description: This course is designed for the interested photography student. Photo I covers all aspects of digital photography within an artistic context. Students will also be introduced to Digital Cameras, Adobe Lightroom, & Photoshop. 35mm photography is accessible for Photo I. Students will learn digital processing, how to print digitally processed photos. Students are expected to work independently, shooting photos after school, at home and during class (when specified). Course work includes shooting assignments, photo history, weekly journals, and a research paper/presentation on a personally selected photographer and the art of photography. Some cameras are available on loan for student use, but it is strongly recommended that you supply your own digital camera if possible.
fulfills_text: Digital Art Requirement

description: This course is designed for the motivated photography student. This is a continuation of the Photography 1 course. It covers all aspects of digital photography while introducing more advanced camera, lighting, and editing techniques. Students will have the opportunity to explore different photographic subjects and printing processes. Studio lighting will be introduced and used to gain a technical understanding of light and camera functions. Emphasis will be placed on independently developed challenges for each project, weekly journals, and monthly “revisits” of missed photographic opportunities. A cohesive portfolio of finished work will be expected of each student at the end of the term, including a digital portfolio. Some cameras are available on loan for student use, it is strongly recommended that the student supply their own digital camera if possible. *This course might also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT

Some cameras are available on loan for student use, but it is strongly recommended that the student supply their own digital camera if possible. *This course might also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT

description: Food Fundamentals will teach you how to be comfortable in the kitchen through hands-on cooperative learning. You will learn about food preparation techniques, proper equipment usage, meal planning, purchasing techniques, nutrition, consumer issues, regional food and foreign food. You will explore the nutrient value in food, how appetite appeal affects what you eat, the social significance of how food plays into our choices, and cultural aspects of food. Students will have opportunities to have community guests in the classroom.
notes: Sub-heading: Family Consumer Sciences (credits satisfy elective requirements)

description: Using the skills learned in Foods Fundamentals students will further develop their skills with more advanced learning, community connections and hands-on food labs. This advanced study is based on nutrition, new food investigation, advanced cooking techniques, and the understanding of where food comes from along with recipe development. Curriculum is based on students interest and skill level.

notes: Sub-heading: Family Consumer Sciences (credits satisfy elective requirements)

description: This class is designed to teach students how professional recordings are made and will give them the knowledge and tools to begin recording themselves at a high level. We will dive into how to use a DAW (digital audio workstation) to record, mix and master music. We will also learn about the different types of microphones, microphone placement, and other recording techniques that lead to high quality recordings. In addition to recording sound in a DAW, we will use midi controllers to create our own music in the class. By the end of this class, students will have an understanding of how to create a high quality recording of singers and instrumentalists. From the initial recording, to production after the fact. They will also learn how to create their own music using a DAW.

description: Students who take this class will learn the basics of rock band instruments such as drums, bass, guitar and keyboard. They will learn from the teacher, peer mentors, and by self-teaching. As students advance their playing skills, they will have the chance to collaborate with one another in listening to songs they like and figuring out how to play the songs themselves. In addition to playing instruments, the class will listen to music from different eras and discuss the history and meaning behind the songs. Students will also have the chance to dabble in using Soundtrap to produce music electronically. Students will have homework and projects as part of this class.
fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

description: Students will learn about and practice different skills that help them to write complete songs. This will include learning about song form/sections, melody, harmony, and rhythm. Students will study parts of language, learning how to use synonyms, adjectives, adverbs, imagery, and syllable count to write great lyrics. They will also work on their singing and learn how to play the guitar and learn what kinds of chord progressions support everyday songwriting. Students will work individually as well as in groups to sing, play, record, and give feedback to one another as they complete a variety of songwriting assignments.
prerequisites: Willingness and ability to sing alone during class.
fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

description: Chorus is a full-year, four-credit class. All chorus members are required to attend all concerts in which the ensemble is performing, including evening concerts in November, March and May. Chorus students are taught about healthy and functional vocal technique, learn music literacy skills, and experience a wide variety of musical styles. Students are placed into sections (soprano, alto, tenor, and bass) and learn to sing advanced harmonies in 4- and 8-parts. Emphasis is placed on diction, dynamics, breath support, register use, expression, and interpretation. The chorus sings songs in many genres, meters, tempos, languages, arrangements and moods. While students learn to sing in a group, they are asked to reflect on their own musical identity and growth through class discussions and assignments. Students enrolling should be prepared to make this year-long commitment to the ensemble they are joining. If a student needs to enroll in Chorus for a single semester for two credits due to a schedule conflict, permission must be granted by the teacher prior to the beginning of the school year. This single semester option does not apply to students in grade nine.
prerequisites: Willingness and ability to participate fully by singing throughout all rehearsals and concerts. Previous chorus experience is highly recommended but not required.
fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

description: Piano and Voice Studio is designed for students who are already BUHS Chorus. This class will meet every other day, opposite of Chorus. We will be learning proper vocal technique and expanding our keyboard skills. We will practice singing and playing our own parts in ensemble music, prepare for auditions, and practice solo works. We will learn how to effectively pick a solo work for your voice level, and how to develop it with guidance of the teacher. description: Band is a full year, four credit class. Band students in all grade levels rehearse and perform together in one band. This performance course is designed to foster an understanding and love of music and music making as well as developing instrumental skills, artistic expression, and creativity. In large and small ensemble settings, band students will explore various musical styles and genres with a focus on standard and contemporary concert band literature as well as arrangements of Broadway and film scores, pop, and rock music. Instrument lessons scheduled during the school day are required for all band members and enable instruction to be differentiated for various instruments and ability levels. Individual achievement is monitored and guided through the use of performance assessments, both in the form of recorded playing tests and live solo performances. A regular routine of home practice is required as is attendance at all group performances, most of which happen outside of the school day. Students enrolling should be prepared to make this full year commitment to the ensemble. If a student needs to enroll in band for a single semester for two credits, permission must be granted by the teacher prior to the beginning of the school year. Students enrolled for a single semester must demonstrate proficiency in all of the performance indicators to earn course credit.

description: Fundamentals of Music is a course dedicated to teaching the basic concepts that all musicians should know. This class is designed for all students, whether or not you are already involved in the music department at BUHS. Students will learn skills and concepts such as how to read notes, read rhythm and navigate a piece of music. We will also spend time learning basic music theory such as how to read a key signature, time signature, and how to build a scale. Listening to music is also a large part of this class. We will learn active listening skills and use them as we listen to music from different time periods in our history. Additionally, we will spend time learning instruments, particularly piano.

description: *Ability to read and play notes as written on a staff. This course is for vocal and instrumental students who are interested in playing jazz. Students will play jazz standards, learning how to interpret and enhance a melody, read chord symbols, drill scale and patterns, and ultimately improvise through a tune. We will also do a lot of listening to the recordings of jazz masters and contemporary musicians, discussing and emulating their singing and playing. We will learn some jazz history in order to understand the origins of this great music and pay our respects to it. Finally, we will learn how to prepare for a jam session or gig, as well as how to work with a band. The class will visit the Vermont Jazz Center to take advantage of their resources and events.

description: Students in this class will take a virtual trip around the world to find out what music is like around the globe! From salsa music to Mongolian Metal to yodeling and K-pop, we explore the characteristics of music from different countries and cultures. In this class, we will learn about the instruments, rhythms, songs and dances associated with world music. We will explore what music from different parts of the world has in common and what makes it distinct. Students in this class should be prepared to listen to music and watch videos, participate in class discussions, and play percussion instruments (no previous experience required).
fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

description: This course is designed to explore the history of Rock ‘n Roll by analyzing, studying and performing its songs. We will be learning about cultural influences on Rock, listening to music representing different stages in its development, and performing songs by major artists. Students will be advancing individual guitar skills for both rhythm and lead guitar as well as discovering the basics of harmony used in Rock ‘n Roll. Guitars will be supplied for students.

description: Visual and Performing Arts Academy students in a music strand must take this class. This course is designed to give students a deep understanding of three fundamental aspects of music theory: rhythm, melody and harmony. A variety of composition projects are designed to follow instruction in these three areas, allowing students to create meaning of the information and apply it in authentic ways. Noteflight music notation program enables students to compose, edit and share their work. Inside Music web-based composition instructional units are used extensively. This rigorous class is best suited for students with some background in music. It is highly recommended for students planning to further pursue music after high school. Topics uncovered include meter, rhythm, time signatures, clefs, pitch notation, major and minor scales, melodic analysis, connections of text to music, motive, form, chords (diatonic and non-diatonic), connection of melody to harmony, chord progressions and analysis.

It is designed to meet the needs of students in accordance with their stages of physical, mental, and social development as well as promote healthy choices. Health Education addresses current issues through units on nutrition & physical activity; bullying & violence prevention; suicide prevention; alcohol, tobacco & other drugs; human sexuality; and healthy relationships. An emphasis is placed on activities designed to build self-efficacy around health skills including decision making skills, goal setting, communication skills, and health advocacy.

course_name: CPR, First Aid & Wilderness First Aid
description: In this hands-on, practical course, students will learn critical life-saving skills that can be applied in everyday situations and emergency scenarios. The curriculum covers three main areas: CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) & AED, basic First Aid, and Wilderness First Aid. Students will gain proficiency in recognizing medical emergencies, using an AED, performing CPR, and providing first aid for common injuries and illnesses. After covering basic first aid techniques, additional emphasis will be placed on first aid techniques in outdoor and remote environments, where professional medical help may be delayed. Key topics include wound care, splinting, hypothermia, heat-related illnesses, snake bites, and other wilderness-specific emergencies. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to respond confidently in both urban and wilderness settings, with the ability to stabilize injured individuals until professional medical help arrives. The course includes certification in CPR and First Aid, ensuring students are well-equipped to handle a wide range of emergency situations. Key Skills Covered: ● Using an AED when one is available ● Performing CPR on adults, children, and infants ● Recognizing and treating common medical emergencies ● Administering first aid for cuts, burns, fractures, and sprains ● Wilderness-specific first aid techniques (e.g., treating hypothermia, insect bites, and dehydration) ● Responding to environmental hazards like extreme heat or cold Grading in this class will be a reflection of active demonstration of learned skills, scores on content-based quizzes, and performance-based role playing of medical emergencies. Active participation will be required.
prerequisites: Health

description: The Vermont Agency of Education (AOE) has established a number of programs through which Vermont high school students can earn both high school and college credit for certain courses they take while in high school. ● “Concurrent” Dual Enrollment (DE) courses are courses taught at BUHS by BUHS faculty who are also adjunct professors with the partner college. These courses are designated in the Programs of Study and on BUHS transcript with an * after the course title. ● “Fast Forward” DE courses are courses taught at WRCC by WRCC faculty who are also adjunct professors with the partner college. They are also designated with an * in the program of studies and on student transcripts. ● “Traditional” DE Courses are taken at the Partner College, either online or on the college campus. These courses are designated by a + symbol in the program of studies and on student transcripts. For a list of eligible AOE Partner Colleges please visit: https://education.vermont.gov/dual-enrollment

description: The Brattleboro Union High School International Studies Academy (ISA) equips students with the knowledge to communicate and participate in an increasingly complex and interconnected world. Students will gain and demonstrate transferable skills that are essential for career readiness and global citizenship in the 21st century. These competencies include: proficiency in a second language; social and intercultural awareness and skills; an understanding of the connections among political, geographical, historical, cultural, religious, and economic systems. Students who successfully complete ISA requirements will receive a designation on their transcripts.
notes: program. Current 8th, 9th, and 10th grade students may apply; requirements listed on pp.22-23

description: AP Computer Science A is a rigorous, college-level programming course that expands on the foundational skills learned in Computer Science 2 or 3. Students will develop proficiency in object-oriented programming using programming language Java while learning to design, implement, test, and refine software solutions to real-world problems. Key topics include creating and using classes and objects, working with complex data structures such as arrays and ArrayLists, developing algorithms that store and process data, and evaluating the efficiency and correctness of different solutions. Students will also examine broader impacts of computing, including responsible use, ethical considerations, and the social implications of software systems. The course concludes with the AP Computer Science A Exam. AP CSA is offered every other year and will run during the 2026–2027 school year.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation andearn a 80% or higher in Computer Science 2 or Computer Science 3
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

description: Computer science touches every part of modern life, and learning to think like a computer scientist – designing solutions, writing programs, tackling challenges – gives you the power to create almost anything you can imagine. Really, it’s like a super power! This course is as much about programming and learning core computer science concepts as it is about creativity, design and problem-solving. We’ll work in Scratch, a block-based programing language ideal for complete beginners as well as those with some programming experience who want a space to explore creative computing. Most assignments project-based, with freedom to design and develop your own original programs. Students earning an 80% or higher are eligible to continue on to Computer Science 2: Programming with Python
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

description: Physical computing forms the basis of smart devices, wearables like smart watches, e-textiles and IoT (Internet of Things) devices. In this semester course, you will learn to design electronic devices that interact with the physical world by building circuits and writing programs that run on microcontrollers (tiny, hand-held computers). You might build a robot arm that can draw, a racetrack that times the speed of a toy car, a small greenhouse that opens a vent if the temperature gets too hot – what you build is up to you! This course is project based and highly self-directed; you will have lots of freedom to pursue your own projects. We will utilize the Arduino microcontroller in projects and the programming language C++.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Computer Science II with at least an 80% or AP Computer Science A with at least a 70%; or demonstrate prior programming experience to the teacher to determine course placement
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

description: In this course, we will learn how to design and build web pages using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and site builders. We’ll examine how thoughtful design choices improve user experience - from making sites more accessible and easier to navigate, to applying principles of visual design to create polished, visually appealing pages. During the first half of the course, we’ll focus on best practices for working with markup languages and learn how to make sites interactive with JavaScript. We’ll also explore how AI tools can support the development of more advanced features. In the second half, our attention will shift toward site builders and design. This is a project-based course with plenty of opportunities to create your own original websites. Students earning an 80% or higher are eligible to continue on to Computer Science 2: Programming with Python.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Curiosity & Creativity

description: Advanced Principles of Engineering is for highly motivated students who are ready and willing to work at a faster pace with greater indepedence. Students will continue to investigate the four areas of technology education with a more in-depth physics emphasis. Students will research, design, and construct projects. Recent design challenges have included constructing parachutes, planes, maglev vehicles, electric terrain vehicles, boats, cutting boards, wooden pens and designing single color screen printing, promotional brochures, architectural layouts, and exploring alternative energy sources (wind, solar, hydro). Class will involve note taking, research, quizzes and tests, but will focus heavily on hands-on projects. This is offered every other year (2026-27, 2028-29), alternating with Principles of Engineering I (2027-28, 2029-30).
prerequisites: Instructor recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication | Also listed on p.94 of main catalog as 'Advanced Principles of Engineering II' (Science & Technology); text differs from this entry

description: Have you taken a design technology course and desire to expand on this learning? Do you have an idea or concept you would like to bring to life? This course is ideal for highly motivated students interested in self-directed learning in the area of design technology and STEAM. Students may choose to study a topic of their choice for a quarter or semester long independent study under the guidance of the design technology teacher. Areas of study may include, but are not limited to: photography, graphic design, architectural design (CAD), silk screen printing, 3D printing, laser technologies, and robotics.
prerequisites: Recommendation of the instructor.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: During this fast-paced semester course, students will learn digital single lens reflex (D-SLR) camera operation, composition, a general history of photography, and photo manipulation through the use of Adobe Photoshop. Projects which teach correct exposure, control of movement, depth of field, photographic perception and the understanding of photographic selection and ‘framing’ will be assigned. This course will involve lectures, demonstrations, critiques and discussions with a heavy focus on hands-on projects.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity. | Also listed on p.42 of main catalog as 'Digital Photography/Imaging' (Fine Arts: Visual Arts); text differs from this entry; prerequisite there: None

description: During this fast-paced semester course, students will explore the graphic design world creating 2D and 3D projects. This course will discuss the visual principles and elements of design. Basic typography, hierarchy of information, and using grid systems for layouts will also be covered. Software training will focus on Adobe Illustrator and Adobe InDesign. Students will also learn the process of silk screen process printing. Students will participate in class critiques, demonstrations, and projects. Class will involve notes, quizzes/tests, and critiques with heavy focus on hands-on projects. Knowledge of Adobe Photoshop is recommended, but not required.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity and Creativity; Effective Communication. | Also listed on p.43 of main catalog as 'Fundamentals of Graphic Design' (Fine Arts: Visual Arts); text differs from this entry

Recent design challenges have included constructing parachutes, planes, maglev vehicles, electric terrain vehicles, boats, cutting boards, wooden pens and designing single color screen printing, promotional brochures, architectural layouts, and exploring alternative energy sources (wind, solar, hydro). Class will involve note taking, research, quizzes and tests, but will focus heavily on hands-on projects.Please note: This class is offered every other year (2026-27, 2028-29), alternating with Principles of Engineering I (2027-28, 2029-30).

notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication; Curiosity & Creativity. | Also listed on p.98 of main catalog as 'Principles of Engineering II' (Science & Technology); text differs from this entry

description: This course is for the highly motivated student wishing to obtain marketable experience in print media publishing. Students will identify and report news-making events; incorporate journalistic forms, create eye-catching layouts, and use photography to document a year in the history of Burlington High School and our community in the annual publication of our yearbook, OREAD. Students must be able to accept responsibility and work independently to meet deadlines. Documentation of events will require that yearbook class members work after school and on weekends. Upon completion of the course students will be able to 1. apply the basic principles of page design and layout 2. operate Adobe InDesign software 3. write copy for captions and text 4. shoot, select, and crop photographs for layout 5. work collaboratively to create a unified theme
prerequisites: Students who request to enroll in Yearbook will be asked to submit a one-page writing sample to Ms. Skoglund answering the following questions: What is the role of the yearbook in a school community? What skills or strengths will you bring to the team?
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: Students in Yearbook II will build on the skills learned in Yearbook I. Students will also learn to edit copy, lead a team to produce articles in a timely fashion, generate new story ideas and feature articles, create slideshows for school events, create marketing campaigns to continue funding the publication’s development, and assume responsibility and leadership for a certain component of the yearbook and publications.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Yearbook I and instructor recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity and Creativity; Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: Students in Yearbook III will build on the skills learned in Yearbook II. Students will also learn to edit copy, lead a team to produce articles in a timely fashion, generate new story ideas and feature articles, create slideshows for school events, create marketing campaigns to continue funding the publication’s development, and assume responsibility and leadership for a certain component of the yearbook and publications.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Yearbook II and instructor recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity and Creativity; Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: The 9th grade English program focuses on three core questions: Who am I? What is my community? How do I fit into the world? We practice three English reading and writing skills: annotation, speaking and listening, and evidence-based writing. This class will be co-assigned and team-taught with Humanities Civics and World Societies. Texts may include: Long Way Down by Jason Reynolds, Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare, Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer, Night by Elie Wiesel, To Kill a Mockingbird by Harper Lee, and Of Mice and Men by John Steinbeck. Earned Honors: Students have the option to earn Honors credit in this class by demonstrating learning throughout the school year at an Honors level. The earned Honors designation will be awarded at the end of year and enables students to take English 10 Honors (Genre) in 10th grade.
fulfills_text: English dept table: 9 Required (4.0 Credits Required in English)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: This course supports continued acquisition of reading and writing skills in preparation for college and careers. The course will broaden students' background in reading, aid them in writing about or responding to a literary selection, and help them build their own vocabulary through the study of words in a literary context. Major works to be studied include but are not limited to: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, Purple Hibiscus, A Raisin in the Sun, When the Emperor Was Divine, The Things They Carried, and Macbeth.
fulfills_text: English dept table: 10 Required (English 10: Lit, Writing, Speech or English 10 Honors: Genre)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: This course is designed for students with a serious interest in the study of literature. Close reading and analysis of fiction are emphasized. Students will read 60-90 pages per week, respond to texts with sensitivity, analyze elements of story and craft, write analytical essays, develop their academic vocabulary, improve their understanding of how language works, and sharpen their discussion and presentation skills. Major works may include The Things They Carried, The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, and Macbeth. To succeed in Genre, students should be able to read and write at grade level and learn independently.
prerequisites: Earned Honors in English 9 with a B- or higher, or teacher recommendation.
fulfills_text: English dept table: 10 Required (English 10: Lit, Writing, Speech or English 10 Honors: Genre)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: This course introduces students to the principles and practice of journalism. Students learn what makes a good story, and how to get the facts through interviews and research. Students are in a constant process of writing and revising to create engaging and informative articles. Units include: the history and ethics of American journalism, newswriting, feature writing, opinion writing, and sports-writing. Introduction to journalism is a required course for students wishing to write for the BHS Register, the BHS print and online newspaper.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication. | Also listed on p.27 of main catalog as 'Journalism I: Introduction to Journalism' (English)

description: In this class students will create the online and print editions of the BHS newspaper “The Register”. As apprentices to seasoned staff, student journalists will continue to practice the skills introduced in Introduction to Journalism. Emphasis is on research, interviewing, and rewriting to achieve mastery. New skills covered include things like digital storytelling and social media strategy. This course is only offered second semester.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Journalism I or teacher recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication. | Also listed on p.28 of main catalog as 'Journalism II: Spring Apprenticeship' (English); text differs from this entry

description: Students in this yearlong course produce the school newspaper “The Register” in both print and online platforms with a focus on fostering professional journalism, enhancing journalistic skills, and empowering students to contribute to a student-run publication. The curriculum encompasses various aspects of journalism, including article writing, conducting interviews, page design, photography, advertisement design, and the creation of broadcast and social media.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Journalism I or teacher recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication. | Also listed on p.28 of main catalog as 'Journalism II: Newspaper & Broadcast' (English); text differs from this entry

description: Students in this course produce the school newspaper “The Register” in both print and online platforms. Students will continue to foster professional journalism while mastering various aspects of journalism, including article writing, conducting interviews, page design, photography, advertisement design, and broadcast media. In addition, students will learn human resource management skills and be expected to take leadership positions as editors and mentors for apprentices.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Journalism II or teacher recommendation.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication. | Also listed on p.28 of main catalog as 'Journalism III' (English); text differs from this entry

description: Can literature capture what it means to be an American? How does it inform our understanding of racial, class, and gender divides? These are some of the questions we will be asking as we engage with a variety of texts spanning the previous century. We will look at poetry, short stories, and novels from the era, placing them in their larger historical and cultural contexts. Close reading and writing will be emphasized throughout the semester. We will study literature with the assumption that art both shapes and reflects culture. Some writers we may read include F. Scott Fitzgerals, Jack Kerouac, and Toni Morrison.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Curiosity and Creativity, Effective Communication.

description: This course offers an introduction to African American literature. Students will read and engage with poetry, short stories, essays, and novels written by African American writers from varied time periods and literary movements as they look for how these texts relate, converse, revise, or depend upon each other. Students will evaluate essays, poems, and novels written by writers such as Zora Neale Hurston, Maya Angelou, James Baldwin, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Toni Morrison and Octavia Butler. We will respond to the works we study with academic essays and creative projects.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: Students explore the darker aspects of human nature through 19th century American stories about the influence of evil, self righteousness, and psychological angst. These worlds are often haunted by female heroines, supernatural elements, and the fears born out of the beginnings of a new nation.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: The AP English Language and Composition course focuses on the development and revision of evidence-based analytic and argumentative writing, the rhetorical analysis of nonfiction texts, and the decisions writers make as they compose and revise. Students evaluate, synthesize, and cite research to support their arguments. Additionally, they read and analyze rhetorical elements and their effects in nonfiction-- including images as forms of texts-- from a range of disciplines and historical periods.This course provides preparation for the AP examination in AP English Language and Composition.
prerequisites: Teacher Recommendation. Completion of a summer assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Personal Development; Effective Communication. | *BHS partners with Saint Michael’s College to offer this course as a concurrent enrollment class. This means that you could earn college credit for this class, in addition to BHS credit. If a student opts in concurrent college enrollment for this course, they will need to submit a dual enrollment voucher form to Saint Michael’s. See Ms. Stein (kstein@bsdvt.org) for details and support.

description: This year-long course is designed for students who want to expand their awareness of language, strengthen their critical reading of poetry and fiction, and further develop their writing style. To understand the power of the written word students will be reading and evaluating the works of established writers, while also writing and evaluating their own writing using the writing process of drafting, editing and revising. Students will be active readers as well as writers, engaging in thoughtful discussions about the role of the writer and the individual in an ever-changing world. This course is concerned with the individual's search for identity, embracing not just the issue of freedom, but also the problems of responsibility and commitment. Novels, short stories, poems and essays are used to examine the themes of fate and free will, illusion and reality, the nature of justice and the question of identity. While examining such themes, students will read critically to determine an author’s purpose, audience, literary strategies, and style and provide evidence of their understanding through class discussions and writings. Students should expect to read and write extensively in this course. This course provides preparation for the AP examination in English Literature and Composition. Major works to be studied may include but are not limited to: Man's Search for Meaning, Blood Dazzler, Slaughterhouse Five, Crime and Punishment, Frankenstein, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, The Stranger, Waiting for Godot, Beloved, and Invisible Man. Students taking this course are able to demonstrate the ability to do college level work by analyzing literature in depth and writing multiple essays of analysis. Completion of a summer assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
prerequisites: Teacher Recommendation

This means that you could earn college credit for this class, in addition to BHS credit. If a student opts in concurrent college enrollment for this course, they will need to submit a dual enrollment voucher form to Saint Michael’s. description: What makes a great movie? Cinema Studies provides the tools to understand and analyze films. We’ll learn about the ways that directors decide on the camera work, set and costume design, and editing to bring their visions to the screen. We will watch films by a variety of directors, each with their own style and approach to storytelling. We will look at how movies have evolved over time. We will analyze camera angles, lighting, sound, and read and write movie reviews. Projects may include storyboarding films, staging photographs to replicate common camera angles and techniques, studying and reviewing a film or a series of films independently, and completing an analysis of a movie’s techniques and values.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

description: This course provides students with opportunities to improve and expand their writing skills. Students will develop an awareness of language, read with more critical understanding, and develop an individual writing style. Writing is a process, which involves prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing. Correct grammar and effective language are a focus of the course. Students read and analyze essays of narration, description, process analysis, comparison and contrast, division and classification, definition, cause and effect, and persuasion and argument. Then, they write their own essays in these styles. This class becomes a writing community where students share and discuss ideas, thoughts, and works. The main focus of this class is writing, but we will also address standards and benchmarks of reading and writing, with an emphasis on writing clear, concise papers that reflect the proper use of the conventions of English.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Curiosity and Creativity; Personal Development.

description: Contemporary literature is often defined as “post-war” (WWII). In this class, students will explore contemporary literature by examining the human experience through texts that belong to and speak to the present. Students drive the lines of inquiry and will read poetry, short stories, and novels, and watch films to gain a deeper understanding of the human condition today. Course proficiencies focus on critical thinking, close reading, and creativity. Students will keep a journal, share their writing and thinking, and formally present their understanding. Units of study may include: post-apocalyptic literature, postmodern storytelling techniques, and a choice-read unit. Core texts may include but are not limited to The Road and Memento.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Curiosity and Creativity, Effective Communication.

description: How do we effectively craft and tell stories? This semester long course is aimed at developing creative writing skills through composition, critique, and revision in an intensive workshop format. Students will explore writing as a process while also sharpening the ability to evaluate creative writings. Students will create short stories, poems, plays, and more. As a class, we will work toward understanding the purposes and motives behind writing. The elements and techniques that go into an effective piece will be constantly analyzed and discussed so that students will perceive some of the various formulas authors use to create immortal, effective art. Students will post and publish work online and in print to reach a wide variety of audiences.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Curiosity & Creativity.

description: This course examines books, speeches, movies, documentaries, and other forms of media centered around topics which have inspired fear in Americans. Through in-depth discussions, we will unpack the role that fear has played in shaping American culture, and attempt to understand the core fears upon which these topics are hinged. Students will practice analytical writing, creative writing and dialogue. Units of study may include War of the Worlds (radio broadcast), Poltergeist, The Bad Seed, Skeleton Crew, “The Lottery,” Psycho, Interview with a Vampire, Baby Teeth, Black Mirror,Twilight Zone, The Final Girl Support Group, The Blair Witch Project, and The Amityville Horror.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving, curiosity and creativity

description: This elective course is designed to give students an in-depth look at both the reading and writing of poetry. Students will examine works by established poets from various movements and cultures throughout the ages. Students will study poetic language, symbolism and themes, as well as voice, style and purpose. Students will engage in reading, reciting and analyzing poetry, as well as creating their own original, poetic works, which will be first edited by a conference partner and then shared with the class upon completion. Proficiency in these areas will be assessed throughout the course.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Curiosity and Creativity; Civic Engagement & Cross-Cultural Understanding.

description: This course will include reading, discussion, and written analysis of several major plays and some of the sonnets. The course explores Shakespeare’s challenging language and the memorable characters that populate his works, including kings, queens, lovers, shrews and fools. Themes such as power, revenge, love, jealousy, ambition and betrayal will be discussed. Critical approaches including psychological, feminist, and historical theories may be presented and applied to the texts.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Creativity and Curiosity, Personal Development

description: Speech class will help students to become more effective and confident public speakers. This class offers students the opportunity to learn the fundamentals of public speaking and to study the basics of communication theory. Students will develop individual speaking styles and study the intricacies of effective speech and improve their writing through a process that includes pre-writing, drafting, revising, and editing. Students will choose their own topics to write with purpose: to inform, to entertain, to argue, and to persuade. Students will also address standards of reading, as we study speeches from history and communication theory. This class values creating a writing community where students openly share and discuss ideas, thoughts, and works.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Personal Development.

description: In this course, you’ll explore how stories work and why they matter to us. We’ll read a wide range of fiction, from classic and contemporary writers like Alice Walker, Octavia Butler, and Samanta Schweblin. You’ll learn how characters develop, how authors build themes, and how point of view shapes meaning. You’ll practice close reading, collaborative annotation, and literary interpretation using different lenses such as feminist, psychological, or historical. Through discussions, writing, and media, you’ll strengthen your critical thinking and discover how stories connect to your own life and identity.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving; Effective Communication.

description: Students read and discuss literature about and by women who have investigated, challenged, and shaped notions of womanhood. This is a survey course. Students read challenging essays, plays, poems, short stories, articles, and novels. Students write extensively, and engage in seminar-style class discussions in this college-preparatory level class. Texts may include Passing by Nella Larsen, The Bluest Eye by Toni Morrison, Woman Warrior by Maxine Hong Kingston, and The Awakening by Kate Chopin.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical thinking and problem solving; Effective Communication

description: World Literature investigates global cultural perspectives about universal human ideas like forgiveness, family, truth, and what it really means “to live a good life.” We will read books and watch films from diverse world creators based on their culture, compare them to each other, and to our own cultural perspective. This is a writing and discussion-based course that will focus on analysis and comparison of ideas, asking you to become cultural investigators and appreciators of perspectives very different from your own.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement Department of Multilingual Learners

description: This course provides basic language instruction to new English language speakers in all four domains. This class is designed for EL students who have very limited English proficiency.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2.

description: This initial reading course provides newcomer students instruction in the foundations of literacy in English. Students will learn the English phonetic systems, early literacy skills, and language needed to continue reading courses at Burlington High School. Students will develop basic reading and comprehension skills.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2.

description: This course develops background knowledge of natural processes and basic scientific concepts, principles, theory, methods, and essential vocabulary. A hands-on approach will be used to establish comprehension.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2 .

description: The goal of this course is to develop background knowledge of world geography and cultures. Students will focus on developing a comprehension of and use of concepts and skills necessary for reading primary sources and non-fiction texts, writing evidence based paragraphs, creating presentations of learning, and participating in research activities in social studies. Social studies concepts will be introduced such as concepts of historical past, timelines and chronology, geographical terms, map usage terms, economic terms, role of culture and concepts of tradition. The proficiencies introduced in this course mirrors the ninth grade social studies proficiencies to facilitate students moving into the mainstream after achieving a foundation of English language and social studies skills.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 2.

description: The goal of this course is to provide basic direct reading instruction to beginning English language learners. This course is designed to assist students in developing English language reading skills. Upon successful completion of Reading 1, and depending on English and language skill proficiency, students will take Supplemental Reading, Lexia, or Reading 2 classes.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 1-2 and/or Lexile level BR0-L100.

description: Year 1 and 2. This is a skills-based class that will focus on strengthening the foundations of reading: decoding, fluency, reading comprehension, and vocabulary. This course will include opportunities for whole class discussions and collaboration, small group work, and independent practice. Everyone can become a better, more successful reader and the goal for this course is to provide the skills and strategies that students can apply across settings to improve their reading and understanding of text. This course will run for a half block each day.
prerequisites: ML Department Recommendation, IXL 0-200, review of SRI Scores and testing data
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication

description: The goal of this course is to provide language instruction to English language learners in order to continue to develop students’ English language proficiency in all four language domains of reading, writing, speaking and listening in English.
prerequisites: ELP Level 2.

description: Students in this course develop background knowledge of U.S. History and Government. Students will focus on developing a comprehension of and use of concepts and skills necessary for reading non-fiction texts and primary sources, writing evidence based paragraphs and participating in research activities in mainstream social studies courses. Students will learn terms related to historical past, timelines and chronology, geography, map usage, economy, government, culture, and concepts of tradition, heritage, history, immigration and migration, freedom, and slavery. This course is designed to meet American History standards for those students who enter BHS having not had an American History class.
prerequisites: ELP Level 2.

description: This course provides reading instruction to English language learners to further develop their English language reading skills. Students will develop vocabulary and writing skills while reading increasingly complex texts.
prerequisites: ELP Level 2 and/or Lexile level BR0-300.

description: The goal of this course is to develop background knowledge of the natural processes as well as the basic scientific concepts, principles, theory, method and essential vocabulary to English learners who lack an educational background or the language necessary for mainstream science. Students in this class will continue to use a hands-on approach to establish comprehension.
prerequisites: ELP Level 2-3. INTERMEDIATE ENGLISH Levels 3-5

description: This course provides language instruction to English learners at an ELP proficiency level 3, in order to advance their development of English in all four language domains and to help students prepare for mainstream English classes. This course will build upon those skills learned in EL English 2.
prerequisites: ELP Writing Level 3.

description: This course provides reading instruction to English language learners to further develop their English language reading skills. Students will develop vocabulary, morphology and comprehension skills while reading increasingly complex texts.
prerequisites: ELP Level 3 and/or Lexile level 200-500.

description: The goal of this course is to provide language instruction to English language learners at a Proficiency Level 3.5 to 4, further advance ELs academic English skills in all four language domains, and help students transition to mainstream English classes. This course also focuses on the 9th and 10th grade English proficiencies of annotating, summarizing and speaking. This course will build upon those skills learned in English Language 3.
prerequisites: ELP Writing Level 4.

description: This class is a support class for English language learners concurrently enrolled in the co-taught 9th grade Humanities and Earth Science. This course will provide students with additional language instruction necessary to succeed in English 9/ Humanities and Earth Science, as well as continue to develop and refine English language skills in speaking, listening, reading, and writing. Placement will be based on reading assessments and will be based on ELL ACCESS scores.
prerequisites: Enrollment in 9th grade Humanities/Civics/Earth Science. ELP Level 3-5.

description: This class supports EL students also enrolled in World History and Biology or Chemistry in order to provide additional instruction, vocabulary and language development, and research assistance to ensure student academic success in mainstream history and science classes.
prerequisites: Enrollment in World History or Biology ELP Level 3.5-5, or other science elective.

description: This supported EL introduction to science course emphasizes laboratory skills and safety. Basic chemistry concepts including matter, compounds, chemical bonding, chemical equations and chemical reactions are included in this course.
prerequisites: ELP Levels 3-4.
notes: Also listed on p.92 of main catalog as 'Introduction to Chemistry' (Science & Technology); text differs from this entry; prerequisite there: Successful completion of Science 2 or equivalent and/or WIDA Level 2-3

description: This course develops background knowledge on the five units in Health Education: Mental Health, Nutrition, Substance Abuse, Relationships and Sexuality. description: This course helps multilingual students prepare for life after high school by exploring college options, career pathways, and workplace expectations. Students build academic English while practicing real-world skills such as goal-setting, resume writing, interviewing, and navigating applications and financial aid. By the end of the course, students create a personalized plan for their post-secondary goals.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This course builds speaking and communication skills for English language learners. Students practice real-world and academic communication through discussions, presentations, and collaborative activities.

description: This introductory singing class is designed for students with little to no formal music ensemble or singing experience. This course is a space for EL students as well as students who have never seen sheet music or made music in a formal group setting before to learn the fundamentals of singing through a variety of songs and genres in a slow-paced, student-driven, and supportive group environment.

description: AP Art History is an introductory college-level art history course. Students cultivate their understanding of art history through analyzing works of art and placing them in historical context as they explore concepts like culture and cultural interactions, theories and interpretations of art, the impact of materials, processes, and techniques on art and art making, and understanding purpose and audience in art historical analysis.
prerequisites: 1 Credit of Visual Art
notes: Student cap: 20 | Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

course_name: Art Foundations (Formerly known as Art I)
description: This semester-long studio course is designed to provide students with the foundational knowledge and skills to practice the creative process of creating, presenting, responding, and connecting through the visual arts. Students will strengthen their discipline literacy of the elements of art as they explore a variety of media, techniques, and design concepts. This course will develop creative thinking and problem solving skills, observational skills, and build self-expression and reflection. Art Foundations is a prerequisite for all upper level art classes.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This is an introductory ceramics course focused primarily on building foundational skills in hand-building and supplemented by opportunities to explore basic wheel-throwing techniques. Students will learn pinch pot, coil and slab construction methods, as well as surface decoration, glazing processes and safe studio practices. Through guided practice and projects, students will gain an understanding of the properties of clay, the stages of the ceramic process, and the artistic possibilities of working in three dimensions.
prerequisites: Successful Completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

description: This is an intermediate course for students who wish to further develop their skills. Students will advance their hand-building abilities, strengthen wheel-throwing techniques, and explore a range of surface treatments and glazing methods. The course emphasizes refined craftsmanship, creative problem-solving, and the development of personal artistic style.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Ceramics I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

description: Drawing 1 is an introductory studio art course that teaches the essential skills of observational and creative drawing. Students explore line, value, proportion, shading, and perspective while working with a variety of mediums. Projects emphasize the elements of art and principles of design, encouraging both technical growth and personal expression. Students will also learn basic critique skills and study selected artists for inspiration. By the end of the course, each student will develop a small portfolio demonstrating improved technique and creativity.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Drawing 2 is an intermediate, studio-based course designed to continue building students’ skills in drawing. Through hands-on practice, students will learn the essential techniques, concepts, and processes used in observational and imaginative drawing. Drawing 2 will be encouraged to find and practice their own style while applying the elements of art and principles of design to demonstrate their understanding of visual literacy. In addition to studio work, students will develop their ability to critique artwork, reflect on their creative choices, and discuss artistic techniques using appropriate vocabulary. By the end of the course, students will have a portfolio of finished drawings that demonstrate technical growth, creativity, and problem-solving.
prerequisites: Drawing I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This introductory studio course in Fiber Arts explores natural and synthetic fiber materials as the primary media to create sculptural artworks. Students will explore a variety of fibers and fiber techniques, focusing on elements of art, principles of design, historical context, and applying it to their own creative expression. Students will study fiber artists and their works, culminating in hands-on projects, critical analysis, and exhibition of their own artworks. Students will build technical skills and vocabulary to successfully pursue upper level fiber art courses.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

description: In this intermediate-level course, students explore a selection of diverse concepts, materials, and processes associated with contemporary fiber arts. Emphasis will be on defining the line between craft and fine art, expanding conceptual development as well as furthering students' technical skills. The course will address the process and development of transforming ideas into form, and pushing the boundaries of traditional craft for visual storytelling.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Fiber Arts I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

course_name: Mixed Media I (Formerly known as Art II)
description: This is a studio course that introduces students to the combined use of drawing, painting, collage and digital media. Students will develop technical skills and creative problem-solving techniques as they explore how multiple materials and processes can be integrated into cohesive artworks. Coursework emphasizes composition, material experimentation, and thoughtful artistic decision-making. By the end of the course, students will complete a portfolio of original mixed-media pieces and gain a deeper understanding of how diverse media can be used to communicate ideas and personal expression.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Drawing I or Painting I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

course_name: Mixed Media II (Formerly known as Art II)
description: This course builds on foundational mixed media skills to help students develop a more personal and sophisticated artistic voice. Through layered exploration of drawing, painting, collage, printmaking, sculpture and digital processes, students learn to combine materials with intention and craftsmanship. Emphasis is placed on creative problem-solving, concept development, experimentation and refining technical skills.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Mixed Media I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Painting 1 is an introductory art course that teaches students the basic skills and techniques of painting. Students learn how to use different painting materials—such as acrylics and watercolors—and explore fundamental concepts like color theory, composition, and brushwork. The class includes guided projects that help students develop creativity, observation skills, and confidence in their artistic abilities.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Painting 2 is an intermediate course designed for students who have completed Painting I and want to deepen their artistic skills. Students explore more advanced techniques in acrylic, watercolor, and mixed media while studying color harmony, style, and personal expression. Projects encourage creativity, problem-solving, and the development of a personal artistic voice. Emphasis is placed on refining technique, experimenting with new approaches, and building a strong portfolio.
prerequisites: Painting I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Printmaking is an introductory art course that teaches students how to create images using a variety of printmaking techniques. Students explore methods such as relief printing, monoprinting, and collagraphs while learning about design, craftsmanship, and safe studio practices. The course emphasizes creativity, experimentation, and developing strong visual ideas.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Sculpture 1 is an introductory studio course in three-dimensional (3D) art making. Students will explore a variety of sculpture techniques with diverse media, including found materials, focusing on elements of art, principles of design, historical context, and applying it to their own creative expression. Students will study sculptors and their works, culminating in hands-on projects, critical analysis, and exhibition of their own artworks. Students will build skills and vocabulary to successfully pursue upper level sculpture courses.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Foundations (formerly known as Art I)
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: In this intermediate-level course, students explore a selection of diverse concepts, materials, and processes associated with contemporary sculpture. Students will experience a variety of additive and subtractive sculpture techniques through various media. Emphasis will be on exploring alternative methods of art production, expanding conceptual development as well as furthering students' technical skills. The course will address the process and development of transforming ideas into form.
prerequisites: Sculpture I
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This introductory guitar class is designed for students with diverse abilities and little or no guitar experience. Utilizing guitars provided by the school and adaptive techniques, students will learn the fundamentals of playing, reading, and writing guitar music in an inclusive and supportive environment.
prerequisites: School-based team referral required.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This course is designed for students who are curious about how music really works, how melodies are built, how harmonies fit together, and what gives music its structure and meaning. AP Music Theory introduces the foundations of harmony and melody as the first year of a college-level music theory sequence. Students begin with essential skills such as note and rhythm reading, intervals, and scales, and then progress to harmonies, chord progressions, ear training, melodic analysis, and composition. By the end of the year, students are prepared to take the Advanced Placement exam, which may allow them to earn college credit, skip a year of college music theory, and/or receive fine arts credit—giving them a strong head start in their musical journey. Successful students typically enter the course with some musical background and basic note-reading skills in at least one clef. While it is strongly encouraged that students in BHS performing ensembles continue in those classes alongside AP Music Theory, since each course supports and strengthens the other, students who are not in a performing ensemble may still enroll and succeed in AP Music Theory. This course is offered every other year (2026-27, 2028-29 etc.).
prerequisites: Successful completion of Music Appreciation (formerly known as Music Theory), one of the ensemble classes, or instructor permission.

description: The Chamber Choir is a select auditioned group that meets weekly before school hours to sing music scored for smaller ensembles. Students will sing Soprano/Alto, Tenor/Bass, and SATB pieces. The group rehearses music from many different genres (acapella, barbershop, musical theater, madrigals, and more) in preparation for several performances during the school year. A strong commitment must be made to rehearsals and to work outside of the regular rehearsal period.
prerequisites: Audition or recommendation from Choir Director is required.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development, Curiosity & Creativity.

description: The Concert Band presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. The Concert Band is open to all students in grades 10-12 who play woodwind, brass, or percussion instruments. The Concert Band studies music from many different historical periods presenting diverse musical styles and genres. This performance ensemble is dedicated to the development of individual instrumental technique and large ensemble skills. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the district, state, and regional levels.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 1 year of Freshman Band
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: The Concert Choir is open to ninth grade and other new singers who wish to participate in the BHS choral program. In addition to performances, members in this group will engage in a program designed to improve their musical skills in rhythm, reading, and technical proficiency on their voice part. This course will include the study of music theory, rehearsal procedure, proper practice habits and a variety of aspects to help strengthen vocal skills. All students interested in singing are encouraged to sign up for this course, even if you do not presently sing.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Calling all string players! The Concert Orchestra is open to all students in grades 9-12 who play violin, viola, cello or string bass. In Concert Orchestra, we study and perform works from the classical genre as well as music from movies, musicals and more! In addition to instruction on their instruments, students will also have brief lessons in music history and music theory to help them become a well rounded musician. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School through music festivals at the state and regional levels. Instruments are provided for those in need.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Digital Music is an introductory course open to all students regardless of music experience. This course is an introduction to the integration of electronics into the world of music creation. Students are taught how to utilize a digital audio workstation, to remix pre existing pieces of music as well as create their own projects from scratch. Students will also be introduced to podcasting and the art of cinema composition. Additionally, students will study composition and recording techniques used by today’s most popular recording artists.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Personal Development, Curiosity & Creativity, Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: The Freshmen Band presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

This course provides a balanced creative and technical theater education for students of any experience level.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: The Jazz Ensemble presents and encourages music performance at Burlington High School. This yearlong co-curricular group meets twice a week in the morning before school and is open to band and orchestra members. Repertoire includes classic big band charts as well as arrangements by contemporary artists. There is a strong emphasis on jazz styles and improvisation. Students are eligible to represent Burlington High School at the Vermont All-State Festival.

notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Curiosity & Creativity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving

course_name: Ethnic Studies: A People’s History Part I
description: This course fulfills 0.5 credits of the American History graduation requirement. This is a semester-based course that provides an opportunity to explore American History through the voices that are often silenced, such as Native Americans, European immigrants, and Latinos. We aim to unpack the social, political and economic implications on America’s development on marginalized peoples in an ethnic studies approach. Our historical timeline of study is from First Contact through Reconstruction. This course has been designed and inspired by historian Howard Zinn’s book, “A People’s History of the United States.” We use both primary and secondary sources to support our learning. Ultimately, the goal is to broaden our understanding of what it means to be a citizen in the United States, as narratives and perspectives have been left unheard. In order to fully appreciate the complex history of this nation, it is vital to recognize all voices that have played a part in America’s development, including their arduous journey.

description: This course fulfills 0.5 credits of the American History graduation requirement. This is a course about America's history through the lens of labor. We will explore the role that organized labor has played in the development of the US and examine the changing nature of work, worker movements, and employment relations in the United States. This is ultimately a US history survey course that seeks to take the lens of labor to cover key moments of US history from its founding to the present day. We will explore and analyze the attitudes, ideologies, cultures, and politics of workers, labor leaders, and employers. This course will also examine how workers of different national, ethnic, racial, and gender backgrounds have experienced work and contributed to the development of unions and worker movements. Other important themes include the rights and responsibilities of employers and workers, the role of the state in the economy and the workplace, the rise and decline of collective bargaining and the New Deal order, globalization and neoliberalism, and the current problems facing workers and the emergence of new worker movements.

description: This course is designed to give students an understanding of political science and how it relates to topics of contemporary history, and an Advanced Placement option for their senior year. It will prepare students for the US Government and Politics exam that students are required to take in May. The course will be taught in a seminar format using materials from both Advanced Placement sources and current events to examine the development of both our structural government and our contemporary political scene. Interwoven into the curriculum of the course are Topics in 20 th and 21st Century History. Examples of topics that may be included are: War and Peace, Colonialism to Globalism, Technological Transformations of the World, the Rise of Fundamentalism, and the Implications of Science in Today’s World.
