description: This course is for self-motivated, serious art students who wish to pursue studies in art further than other courses have allowed. College bound students may use this time to accumulate work for a college portfolio. Other students may have a particular media that they want to explore in-depth. Projects and topics of study are proposed by the students, although some assignments may be given. In addition to studio projects, students will submit weekly sketchbooks and writing assignments. Writing topics will include art processes, art history, art criticism, current events, and moral/ethical questions in art. Emphasis is placed on skill, creativity, problem solving, experimentation, self-direction and self-critique. The product of the semester’s work will be an exhibition which communicates a progression of skills and ideas.
prerequisites: Students will have taken a minimum of two art courses. More consideration will be given to students who have taken more than one Foundations and all offered Upper Level courses.

course_name: EC Intro to Business Logic & Ethics
description: This course will incorporate logic and problem solving with various business applications to deal with ethical issues. Case problems will be systematically analyzed to better understand the concepts involved in making business management decisions. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.
prerequisites: None
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC MGMT112W, 3 credits.

description: Students will explore the dynamic world of modern technology through hands-on experiences in podcasting, video production, and digital storytelling. Students will learn the basics of audio and video production, including scripting, recording, editing, and publishing content across digital platforms. They will also gain an understanding of responsible digital citizenship, media literacy, and the impact of technology on communication and society. Projects will include creating original podcasts, filming and editing short videos, and engaging with industry-standard tools and software.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard). The course-selection lists (pp.28-31) call this 'Intro to Technology & Social Media' and list 'Intro to Technology & Digital Media' as a ninth-grade elective.

description: The focus will be on both marketing theory and practice. The text will introduce consumerism, pricing, motivation, and sales promotion. The student will be responsible for writing a marketing plan for the school store and implementing parts of the plan. This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.
prerequisites: None
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC MGMT212W, 3 credits.

description: This course involves students in the process of creating a publication. It integrates graphic design, desktop publishing, digital photography, finance, online activities and public relations. The major production is the yearbook and/or supplement to the yearbook. Due to the nature of the product, students taking the course are expected to be responsible and self-motivated. This is a FULL year course.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: This course will explore the richness of American literature as well as the stories that caused them to be written. The course will explore Native American and early colonial writings and then branch out into the giants of the 19th and 20th centuries before ending with modern American classics. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Crucible, The Scarlet Letter, various short works and poetry by Poe and others, The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, The Grapes of Wrath, The Old Man and the Sea, Our Town, Death of a Salesman, and The Things They Carried. Non-fiction reading will come in the form of articles, research, etc. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 9th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/ explanatory, argumentative, and narrative. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; American Literature required for graduation
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical areas: Early Medieval, Gothic, the Italian Renaissance, Fifteenth Century Art in Northern Europe, Art of Sixteenth Century Europe, Baroque, and Rococo. Even in an era dubbed the “Dark Ages”, people produced amazing works of art. From painting illuminated manuscripts to the construction of light filled cathedrals, the artists of these time periods demonstrated advanced skills and shed light on their subjects during some very adverse and challenging times. Their works of art will serve as the inspiration for students as they develop technical skills and create their own drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, and other applied works of art.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). The catalog prints, as this course's description, the same text as the Art Illuminates the Dark art course (apparent copy-paste error in the source); copied verbatim.

description: In this course, students will focus on developing creativity through original forms of descriptive writing, poetry, drama and fiction. Vivid vocabulary development, and creative writing techniques will be explored while working on essential worldbuilding skills. Students will have opportunities to take part in writing contests and to submit their work on the Young Writer's Project website. Elements of fiction and poetry writing will include character development, setting, plot, sensory details, imagery, figurative language and sound devices. Among the units considered for this course are Modified Fairy Tales, Gothic Literature, Fantasy, Science Fiction, Media Critique, Realistic, and Adventure. (Course is offered in the Fall.)
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
offering_note: Course is offered in the Fall.
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course provides an introduction to the principles of writing and organizing stories for publication in print and electronic mediums, as well as getting students ready for the transition into the career world. Students will develop and compose news stories, learn and adhere to industry-standard style guidelines, conduct meaningful and appropriate research, and understand how the ethics, laws, and culture of journalism influence the media. Students will also create a working resume, cover letter, and work on college admissions essays. (Course is offered in the Spring.)
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
offering_note: Course is offered in the Spring.
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course will explore modern literature from the 20th and 21st centuries. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, The Grapes of Wrath, Death of a Salesman, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, The Devil in the White City and In Cold Blood. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 10th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/explanatory, argumentative, and literary analysis. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and participate. The honors course differs from the standards in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Also, some literature selections will differ.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This elective upper level course is designed to expand students' literary horizons beyond their English and American heritage to include the study of masterworks of world literature. Students will come to a greater appreciation of and reverence for “foreign” cultural traditions, values, and attitudes, while at the same time identifying those elements which bind all humans together. Students will utilize critical reading and thinking skills, increase their knowledge of vocabulary, develop expository writing skills, produce a research paper, and engage in team learning activities. Students will read a variety of texts, both fiction and nonfiction, from global authors both modern and historical. Reading selections will come from Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, East Asia, and Eastern Europe. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 11th grade writing and reading as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading and the amount and length of writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course deals with physical, emotional, social and mental well-being. It looks at you as a healthy, whole person. The main topics discussed are: family health, mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, personal health habits, consumer health, substance abuse, and birth control information. Expectations of the course include: class participation, personal reflection, fitness days, and public speaking.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Health is required for graduation
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Standard: This first-year algebra course is designed to help students develop an understanding of variables, linear and quadratic functions, exponents and exponential functions, radicals, factoring, and polynomials. Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem solving. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This is a fast paced first-year Algebra course designed to help students develop an understanding of variables, exponents, radicals factoring, polynomials, and rational expressions. Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem-solving skills.
prerequisites: Standard: Score of 60+ on the Algebra readiness assessment 232 on NWEA testing; Honors: Score of 70+ on the Algebra readiness assessment, Pre-Algebra 85%, or 238 on NWEA testing
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

description: Standard: This course is a continuation of Algebra. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics will include in-depth work with quadratics, polynomial functions, their properties, and applications. Trigonometric functions, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, rational equations, probability and statistics will be explored. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This course is a continuation of Algebra I Honors. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics include working with basic functions, their properties, and applications, trigonometric functions, analytic geometry, systems of equations, polynomials, relations and functions of the first, second, and third degree, real exponents, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, probability and statistics.
prerequisites: Standard: Algebra I (Standard or Honors); Honors: Algebra I Honors - a student who takes a full year or two semester to complete Algebra I is not eligible for Algebra II Honors.
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

description: Topics covered include trigonometry, logarithms, analytic geometry, limits and continuity, differentiation of all types of Algebraic functions, inverse functions, concepts of integration, including basic tools for integrating on both the open and closed interval. Strong emphasis will be placed on the application of these skills. This course will be offered in the spring.
prerequisites: Pre-Calculus or Instructor recommendation
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
offering_note: Alternating Course: Offered 2026-2027; offered in the spring
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.18) maps it to WMCC 'Calculus I' MATH215W, 4 credits.

description: Standard: The concepts of two and three-dimensional geometry are integrated throughout the course. A major goal of the course is to help students develop logical methods of thinking. The topics also include coordinate geometry, geometric figures, triangles, surface area, volume, circles and trigonometry. Honors: This course places equal emphasis on geometric theory and application. The concepts of two and three-dimensional geometry are integrated throughout the course. A major goal of the course is to help students develop rigorous and logical, systematic methods of thinking. Therefore, proofs, and constructions are emphasized. The topics also include basic figures, proofs, coordinate geometry, constructions, and trigonometry.
prerequisites: Standard: Algebra I Standard; Honors: Algebra I Honors
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

description: Life Skills Math should not be taken for credit after a student passes Algebra 1. It is an introductory course for students that need remediation of basic math skills. Life Skills Math provides learners with math skills related to activities of daily living. Students will participate in a simulation of real-life mathematical issues, including earning money through a job, writing checks and paying bills with other forms of payment. Topics explored include identifying numbers as they relate to daily living, basic computations, understanding money value concepts, budgeting, measurement, time management, graphic representation, and elapsed time.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: This course will inform students how individual choices directly influence occupational goals and future earnings potential. Real world topics covered will include income, money management, spending and credit, as well as saving and investing. Students will design personal and household budgets utilizing checking and saving accounts, gain knowledge in finance, debt and credit management, and evaluate and understand insurance and taxes. This course will provide a foundational understanding for making informed personal financial decisions leading to financial independence.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Personal Finance is required for graduation
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Also listed as a Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Business Administration & Technology (p.59).

description: This course is a prerequisite for Algebra 1. Topics covered include operations with fraction, decimals, radicals, linear equations in one and two variables, applications, graphing, elementary geometry, proportions and ratios, including percent problems, and problem-solving skills.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Grade placement column: 'Typically taken during 9th grade'.

description: This course develops those topics required to prepare a student for a Calculus course. There is a strong emphasis on the algebra of functions, especially as they apply to trigonometry. Topics include geometric concepts, trigonometry, identities, vectors, exponents and logarithms, graphing techniques, analytic geometry, complex numbers, limits and continuity, and sigma notation. Applications and pattern recognition will be emphasized. This course should be offered in the fall.
prerequisites: Algebra I, Algebra II, Geometry Honors
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
offering_note: Alternating Course: Offered 2026-2027; offered in the fall
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC MATH180W, 4 credits.

description: Quantitative Reasoning is a course for students that do not see themselves going into a math/science related college program. This course covers a variety of topics which will provide a foundation for further courses in mathematics as well as other academic areas. Topics covered include set theory, logic, algebra, linear equalities and inequalities, the metric system, financial math, probability, and an introduction to trigonometry.
prerequisites: Algebra I, Algebra II, Geometry (Honors Recommended)
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC MATH120W, 4 credits.

description: This introductory statistics course will cover topics such as methods of obtaining, analyzing and presenting data, elementary probability, probability distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, linear regression and correlation. A TI-84 Graphing Calculator is required.
prerequisites: Algebra I, Algebra II, For Early College, per WMCC, Quantitative Reasoning is recommended, but not necessary
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC MATH214W, 4 credits.

description: This course covers three major modules: ● Music Theory/Songwriting - students will gain an understanding of the fundamental building blocks of music. They will learn how to read rhythms and notes, as well as building chords, writing melodies and composing their own music. ● World Music - students will gain an understanding of music in different world cultures. They will understand how music is important in different communities and gain hands-on experience playing the music in an authentic fashion. ● Music in Media - students will learn how to create music for various forms of media, including movies, video games, and advertisements. They will gain an understanding of techniques used to engage an audience and play with their emotions.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: One credit required for graduation (Music)
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Adapted Physical Education is an academic course designed to expose students to various activities and sports (at an adapted level based on the student’s needs) that promote an active, healthy lifestyle as well as are aligned with the Society for Health and Physical Education (SHAPE) academic standards. Students will explore the history, strategies, skills and rules of various recreational activities such as: Locomotor, Spatial awareness, sports skills, and health related fitness. Other sports and activities may be introduced as time, equipment and class size allow. Also, students will understand and employ ways to improve health related physical fitness. Students will become familiar with the components of health-related physical fitness which include cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, body composition and muscular strength and endurance. The “Fitnessgram”or (Brockport Fitness test) battery of tests and various technology products will be used to let students self-assess their health related fitness levels on a monthly basis. Students will be expected to dress in appropriate clothing for physical activities unless otherwise directed by the instructor. Most units will entail some skills recognition assessments, written assessments. Other assignments may include: Internet research, fitness journaling, and best course of action mini-reports related to the PE subject area. Class participation, social maturity and a positive attitude are paramount for being successful in this class. Outside class work will be 3hrs. per week maximum. “Fitness for Life, 6th ed.” will be furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assessments if appropriate with the students’ needs. If a student could not perform book work, alternate cognitive assignments will be created based on the level of the student.
prerequisites: Be recommended by a Case Manager, Specialist, or Director of Student Services
notes: Level listed: Modified (Level 2).

description: Adapted Physical Education 2 is an academic course that builds on mastering the SHAPE standards indicated in APE - I as well as the principles, strategies and teachings learned in Adapted Physical Education 1. Outside class work for this particular course will be no more than 3 hours per week. Unit study guides and a textbook entitled Aerobic Fitness Everyone will be furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assignments. If a student could not perform book work, alternate cognitive assignments will be created based on the level of the student. All course materials will be adapted based on the class, or the individual student.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Adaptive PE I, or be recommended by a Case Manager, Specialist, or the Director of Student Services
notes: Level listed: Modified (Level 2).

description: Fitness students will learn about physical fitness, the important role that exercise plays in our lives and how we can safely incorporate exercise into our daily routine. Concepts covered are related to nutrition, proper stretching and cooling down, strength and cardiovascular training, prevention and first aid for sports injuries, and fitness for special populations.
prerequisites: Successful completion of PE I or equivalent
notes: Level 2 (Standard). The course-selection lists (pp.28-31) call it 'Personal Fitness/Sports Skills & Recreational Activities'.

description: Physical Education is an academic course designed to expose students to various activities and sports (at an intermediate level) that promote an active, healthy lifestyle as well as are aligned with the Society for Health and Physical Education (SHAPE) academic standards. Students will explore the history, strategies, skills and rules of various recreational sports such as: Ultimate Frisbee, team handball, archery, orienteering, badminton, Pickleball and volleyball. Other sports and activities may be introduced as time, equipment and class size allow. Also, students will understand and employ ways to improve health related physical fitness. Students will become familiar with the components of health-related physical fitness which include cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, body composition and muscular strength and endurance. The “Fitnessgram” battery of tests and various technology products will be used to let students self-assess their health-related fitness levels on a monthly basis. Students will be expected to dress in appropriate clothing for physical activities unless otherwise directed by the instructor. Most units will entail some skills recognition assessments, written assessments and group project work. Other assignments may include: Internet research, fitness journaling, and best course of action papers related to the PE subject area. Class participation, social maturity and a positive attitude are paramount for being successful in this class. Outside class work will be 3 hours per week maximum. Unit study guides and a textbook entitled “Fitness for Life” will be furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assessments.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Course-selection lists (p.28) show PE I as the required freshman physical education course. A PE II is named in the selection lists (pp.28-31) but has no entry in the course offerings.

description: Students who enroll in this course will be expected to have an independent focus on mastering various SHAPE academic standards through some of the following suggested options: ● Tae-Kwon-Do ● Attend Basic Training (if joining the military) ● Dance lessons ● Weight-lifting The above options would be graded on a pass/fail basis; no number grade will be recorded. Activity type and duration of participation in activity will require verification from an approved course mentor. This course requires the student to develop a learning contract and design an independent project, and in some cases identify a member of the community to work with. This contract requires the approval of the PE teacher and the principal
prerequisites: Successful completion of PE I or 1 transfer credit from another school
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Independent study.

description: Sports Skills and Recreational Activities is an academic course designed to afford students the opportunity to engage in and study various skills for sports and lifetime recreational activities. Students will explore the history, strategies, skills, and rules of various recreational sports such as: Ultimate Frisbee, team handball, basketball, football, badminton, Pickleball, volleyball, pillo-polo/field hockey, and soccer. Other sports and activities may be introduced as time, equipment, and class size allow. Students will be expected to work towards improving skills in all sports studied, as well as designing and running class tournaments. Students will experience opportunities that promote physical literacy and lifetime wellness. Some units will be delivered by the instructor to the students via NFHSLEARN.COM and others will be study guides furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assessments.
prerequisites: Successful completion of PE I or equivalent
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Modified & Standard: Biology is the study of all living things, how they are different, reproduce, grow and live in their surroundings. Weekly laboratory activities will be conducted to reinforce topics studied in the classroom. Honors: This biology class is for students who are considering attending a two or four-year post-secondary institution. Topics of study include biochemistry, genetics, evolution, and ecology. Weekly laboratory experiments will be conducted to reinforce lecture topics.
prerequisites: Modified & Standard: None; Honors: B or higher in Conceptual Physics and Conceptual Chemistry, Algebra I, and instructor's permission
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Physics, Chemistry, and Biology are required for graduation (starting with Class of 2027)
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission for Early College)'; the course-selection lists (pp.29-31) also show Biology for incoming sophomores.

description: Conceptual is designed to introduce students to key topics in chemistry; providing them with a foundation for future science courses. Conceptual Chemistry differs from a more traditional chemistry course in that the focus is on chemical concepts and qualitative laboratory analysis. The goals of Conceptual Chemistry are to develop a conceptual framework for modern chemistry and to allow students to gain experience and appreciation of chemistry through experimentation and inquiry. Students in this course will learn practical scientific skills used to investigate and explore the modern world.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Fulfills the Chemistry requirement
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Practical chemistry is a course that will demonstrate the vital role chemistry plays in everyday life. Students will learn about matter and its properties, the atom, the periodic table, chemical reactions and acids and bases through hands-on activities and real-life examples. Because chemistry can be abstract, this course will use concrete applications to help students comprehend the hypothetical. Students will develop problem-solving skills through the application of chemical concepts to real-world situations.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Fulfills the Chemistry requirement
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Conceptual Physics is an introductory science course designed to prepare students for all future high school science courses. Physics is the basic science. It is the foundation for all other sciences. Since individuals are forced to interact with the physical world around them daily, they need to understand the rules of nature that govern their physical world. While the rules of nature are often described mathematically, it is not the only way to describe them. Conceptual Physics emphasizes learning the fundamental principles of nature from which these concepts are derived. For example, mathematics is not necessary to understand that energy is neither created nor destroyed. This concept is one of the fundamentals of physics. In this course, the focus will be on concepts, ideas, and scientific thinking rather than on high level mathematics. A student only needs to have basic math skills to be successful in this course. Therefore, at the completion of Conceptual Physics, students will have a strong foundational knowledge of the laws that govern the universe and how to apply them to everyday situations.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Fulfills the Physics requirement
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Practical physics is a course that will focus on exploring the laws of physics in the context of everyday life and experiences. It will help students understand the fundamental concepts of speed, velocity, acceleration, forces, motion, work, power, and energy and how they apply to their daily lives. Hands-on activities and labs will be used to reinforce and illustrate these concepts and provide students with a deeper understanding of them. This course will focus on using critical thinking skills to help students develop a qualitative understanding of physics rather than focusing on complex mathematical formulas.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Fulfills the Physics requirement
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

course_name: EC Dendrology & Introduction to Tree and Shrub Identification
description: Dendrology is the study of trees and other woody plants. In Dendrology and Introduction to Tree and Shrub Identification, students learn the taxonomy, geographic range, natural history, ecological relationships, and uses of major tree and shrub families found in New England. Laboratory work focuses on the morphology and classification of common New England trees and shrubs. In the field, the emphasis is on identification. This course is an embedded year-long course within the Diversified Agriculture and Natural Resources program.
prerequisites: None
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.19) maps it to WMCC FRST101W, 4 credits.

description: Forestry Resources introduces students to a wide range of issues that forests face in a changing climate with a growing human population. These interactions between humans and forests are extensive. Humans place significant pressures on forest resources, expecting many services in return. This course explores these interactions and other forestry-related topics, including distribution and forest ecology, silvics and forest management, and ecosystem services. This course also addresses alternative uses for forests and solutions to forestry-related issues. This course is an embedded year-long course within the Diversified Agriculture and Natural Resources program.
prerequisites: WMCC recommends Dendrology & Intro to Tree & Shrub Identification
provider: White Mountains Community College (Early College at Your High School)
notes: Grade placement printed as '11-12 (10 with instructor permission)'. Level 4 (Early College). Catalog's approved list (p.20) maps it to WMCC FRST205W, 4 credits.

description: In this course students will acquire the skills and knowledge necessary to become responsible and effective citizens and consumers in an interdependent world. Civics topics covered include the American government, political parties, law, crime and punishment, and citizenship. Economic topics include supply and demand, businesses and the stock market, value and exchange systems, and others. Grades will be based on quizzes, exams, research-based projects, presentations, and general class work.
prerequisites: At least two social studies credits (including Early U.S. History)
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: This course is designed to focus on events from US history from the pre-Columbian era to the conclusion of the Civil War and Reconstruction. The course emphasizes how European contact with the New World shaped the development of cultural, economic, and political institutions from colonial times to the present. Also of importance is the coming of the revolution and the consolidation of the republic, the expansion of democracy, and westward movement across the country. Students are expected to participate fully in class through note taking, discussion, and classwork assignments. Grades will be based on quizzes, exams, research projects, presentations, general coursework, and participation.
prerequisites: World History or World Events and Geography (or equivalent 1 credit course)
fulfills_text: Fulfills the U.S. History requirement
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). U.S. History is required for graduation.

description: This course will chart the history of the United States from the end of the Civil War to the dawn of the twenty-first century. Major themes include migrations to and within the country, economic transformations, the rise of the US as a world power, the evolution of the role of the federal government, and the long struggle for individual and group rights. The course strives to understand these changes and conflicts through the perspective of a variety of people’s everyday experiences and concerns.
prerequisites: World History or World Events and Geography and Early US History
fulfills_text: Fulfills the U.S. History requirement
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). U.S. History is required for graduation.

description: This course is a broad introduction to the field of psychology. Students will explore the key figures, diverse theoretical perspectives, and research findings that have shaped some of the major areas of contemporary psychology. This course also examines the research methods used by psychologists across these areas to study the origins and variations in human behavior. Grades will be based on quizzes, exams, a research project, and general course work.
prerequisites: Earned at least 2 social studies credits. Recommended NWEA reading level of at least 220
notes: Level listed: Honors (Level 3). The course-selection lists call it 'Psychology Honors'.

description: This class is intended as an introductory social studies course with an emphasis on basic social studies knowledge including geography, economics, and causes of conflict. This course will look at world events through the filter of geography using the themes of location, place, movement, human-environmental interaction, and regions. Students will use maps, conduct research, write essays, give presentations, as well as demonstrate geographic understanding through general course work.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Entry adds: 'Strongly recommended for Freshman year'.

description: This course will look at world events from the origin of early humans and non-human primates and will end with the Renaissance and Reformation periods. This course will cover evolution, early societies and civilizations, kingdoms and empires, the achievements of the classical world, and the transition into the early modern era. Students’ grades will be based on reading, quizzes, exams, essays, research papers, and other projects.
prerequisites: None
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: Driver’s education is an essential first step to lifelong driving skills and is one of the first major responsibilities in a teenager’s life. This course teaches basic traffic laws, rules of the road, basic motor vehicle operation, driver awareness, and drug and alcohol effects on driving. This course is offered each spring.
prerequisites: Must be 16 years old by June 30 for NH students. Must be 15 years old by April 1 for VT students. VT students must provide their learner’s permit number prior to the start of the course.
notes: Level 2 (Standard).

description: This 5-day/week LNA licensure program will take place at the Coos County Nursing Home in West Stewartstown, New Hampshire. Students will be scheduled for their block one class. Students will get 60 hours of theory (lecture), 70 hours of clinical (hands on) for sufficient course hours to test and apply for LNA licensure with the state of New Hampshire. The school district will pay for all costs associated with the course including the workbook, criminal record check, the state exam and licensing fees. The cost of the medical physical is the student’s own responsibility. Students are also responsible for transportation back and forth from the nursing home and school. Enrollment maximums will vary year-to-year. Students from Colebrook Academy and Pittsburg High School participate as well.
prerequisites: Must be 16 years old when the course starts. For acceptance into the program, students must write a short essay on “why I want to be an LNA”; pass a test that indicates ability to read and write English and has decision-making/judgement skills; provide 3 letters of references (unrelated) who can vouch for character, reliability and integrity; have a physical done by a medical provider and undergo a tuberculin skin test.
provider: Coos County Nursing Home, West Stewartstown, New Hampshire
notes: Level listed: Honors (Level 3). Students from Colebrook Academy and Pittsburg High School also participate.

description: This course is recommended for a student interested in enrolling in the Building Trades CTE Program. Through the use of computer-aided drafting, field trips to construction sites and examination of trade journals and drawings, students will learn the varied construction industry. Students will study architectural styles and the evolution of technology in construction. Students will design, estimate and schedule phases of the Building Trades project. Upon completion of the course, students will be able to read and interpret blueprints, understand permits, building codes and develop the skills necessary to plan a building project. The following areas will be emphasized: Project planning; Construction estimating; Heavy equipment / Site selection; Permits / Zoning / Building codes; Architectural drafting; Residential and Commercial construction; Internet resources; Mechanical and Electrical systems.
prerequisites: None
notes: Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Integrated Trades (subheading). Level 2 (Standard).

description: This course is recommended for a student interested in enrolling in the Building Trades CTE program. This course is designed to give students the basic skills necessary to make minor repairs around the home. Through a series of projects and exercises, students will learn the use of portable power tools and hand tools. Students will demonstrate basic knowledge of plumbing and electrical systems in the home. This course will cover topics from changing a furnace filter, sharpening a lawn mower blade to patching holes in drywall. The following areas will be emphasized: Home safety; Portable power and hand tools; Electrical systems; Plumbing and Heating Systems; Painting and interior finishes; Building Materials and fasteners; Weatherization and energy savings. Upon completion of this course, students will have the knowledge of what is necessary to maintain and repair the various systems in a home. Through this course students will be exposed to some of the many trades in the construction industry. Carpenter, Plumber and Electrician are some of the skilled trades students will be introduced to. Students will be graded on bringing a job to completion in an efficient and craftsmen-like matter. It is to be understood that the completed job must be at an industry standard that is to be determined by the instructor. Students are graded along the way to job completion and not just on the finished product. Tasks will be graded during the job process, which includes safety, material use, time management and problem-solving ability. Students will be responsible to follow all class rules and class policy that are distributed at the beginning of the school year and reviewed with the instructor, students and parents. Everyone must recognize that the shop is much different than a classroom and proper attitude must be maintained at all times.
prerequisites: None
notes: Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Integrated Trades (subheading). Level 2 (Standard). Called 'Home Repair' in the course-selection lists.

description: This course is recommended if a student is interested in enrolling in either the Advanced Integrated Manufacturing or Building Trades Program. This hands-on course is designed to give students the basic skills and knowledge necessary to create a project out of wood. Through a series of projects and lessons, students will learn the use of hand and power tools and finishing methods. The following areas will be emphasized: Shop safety; Machine/Tool safety; Fraction and ruler skills and Creativity.
prerequisites: None

Students will be required to design and construct their own project. The projects will require more difficult construction methods such as doors & drawers. As in Woodworking I, the following areas will be emphasized: Shop safety; Machine/Tool safety; Fraction and ruler skills; Basic Drafting skills and Creativity.

Also, students may be required to build and display one item that will be auctioned off at the end of the course. The following areas will still be emphasized: Shop safety; Machine/Tool safety; Fraction and ruler skills; Drafting skills and Creativity.

description: Students enrolled in this course are provided with an overview instruction with a focus on firefighter personal protective equipment, fire behavior, building construction, fire suppression, EMS culture of safety, patient assessment and treatment skills. Just as in the actual Emergency Services CTE courses, students will learn to demonstrate problem-solving and critical thinking skills to analyze, synthesize and evaluate situations independently and in teams. Students may have the opportunity to earn Wildland Firefighter certification via VT Agency of Natural Resources and the VT Fire Academy. They will also have an introduction to emergency scene management and may have an opportunity to earn National Incident Management Systems certifications. Initial exploration of Emergency Service will include classroom work (lectures, readings, skills, practicals) and visits with local experts in the field. Students may participate in a ride-along with local first responders and fire departments per the authority of the department chief’s permission and school administration

description: The Business Administration and Technology (BAT) Program is designed to equip students with the essential knowledge and skills needed for success in today’s competitive business environment. Through a combination of hands-on learning experiences, dual-credit course opportunities, and involvement in real-world business operations, students are prepared to enter the workforce or continue their education at a postsecondary institution with confidence and competence. Students in this program develop a strong foundation in business principles, financial literacy, marketing, entrepreneurship, accounting, and technology applications. They gain practical experience that mirrors real business operations, enhancing their understanding of the professional world and the expectations of today’s employers. A key component of the program is active student participation in the school store, a dynamic, student-run enterprise. This experience gives students first hand exposure to concepts such as cost and profit analysis, customer service, inventory management, accounting, marketing, advertising, and more—valuable skills that translate directly into workplace readiness. Additionally, students become members of Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA), the nation’s premier business career student organization. FBLA’s mission is to inspire and prepare students to become community-minded business leaders in a global society through leadership development, academic competitions, and career preparation events. Whether entering the workforce immediately after high school or pursuing a college degree, graduates of the Business Administration and Technology Program leave with a competitive edge, a professional mindset, and a comprehensive understanding of the business world.

YEAR 2 (9 college credits): RS Accounting I; RS Marketing; RS Business Software Applications; CTSO Membership: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA); School Store/Student Lounge. Students will be issued their own medical kits to train with to apply skills training and preparation for patient assessment and care for the sick and injured including adults, pediatrics and geriatrics. Students will participate in career specific training with the 45 th EMS and the Upper Connecticut Valley Hospital Emergency Department via professional training preceptor agreements.

description: The Integrated Trades program is a dynamic, hands-on course that merges key elements from the former Building Construction & Restoration Carpentry (BT) and Diversified Agriculture & Natural Resources (DAgNR) programs. Designed to prepare students for entry-level employment or further education, this program provides a comprehensive experience in both the construction and agricultural trades through immersive, real-world learning. Students will engage in every phase of construction work, from deconstruction to finish carpentry, gaining essential job-site experience and learning to navigate building renovations with confidence. In addition to construction, students will explore modern agricultural and natural resource industries. These experiences help students develop entrepreneurial thinking, communication, and decision-making skills. The program takes place almost entirely in a real-world, job site or outdoor setting, such as the Canaan Community Forest, while emphasizing safety, professionalism, and workplace readiness. Students should be prepared to work outdoors in all weather conditions and must have appropriate gear and a strong work ethic. Safety is prioritized in all activities, especially those involving equipment such as chainsaws, tractors, and power tools. Students also have the opportunity to participate in the National FFA Organization, a nonprofit career and technical student organization (CTSO) dedicated to promoting career success for students in the Agriculture, Food, and Natural Resources career cluster. FFA is student-led, dynamic, and determined to help students grow personally, as well as develop critical career and leadership skills. It accomplishes this through national events, programs, contests, and more.

fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Math credit and 1 Science credit upon completion of program

Dual-Enrollment Opportunities: Dendrology and Intro to Tree & Shrub Identification (4 credits); Forestry Resources (4 credits). Industry-Recognized Certifications: OSHA-10; American Heart Association AED/CPR First Aid Certification; Game of Logging (Chainsaw Safety) Levels 1, 2, 3, and 4; Man Lift Certification; National Safe Tractor and Machinery Operation Program (NSTMOP); Powder Actuated Tools Certification; 30-Hour Welding Course through White Mountain Community College. By integrating both construction and natural resource-based trades, the Integrated Trades program offers students a broad skill set and exposure to a wide range of career paths, all taught through experiential, hands-on learning. program

description: Concurrent College and High School Credit Opportunities For Vermont Residents (VT DE) allows high school juniors and seniors to take up to two college courses for free at participating postsecondary partner schools. These classes are weighted as heavier than Honors courses and are designated on transcripts with “DE” at the end of the course name. For example, (CCV) Law Enforcement in America - DE indicates that it was a dual enrollment class through Community College of Vermont (CCV). Students can take courses during the summer of his/her junior year through the spring semester of his/her senior year. The program is only available to students who are Vermont residents. There are currently 19 participating colleges throughout the state. To find out more about this program, see http://www.vtdualenrollment.org. Accommodations are allowable; however, DE coursework cannot be modified. If a student withdraws from a DE course after the add/drop deadline at CMHS but prior to the college’s, the high school will enter a “W” and the course will remain on the high school transcript. Students who withdraw from a DE course will continue in a non-DE version of the course or an alternative option (like an independent study) which will be added to the schedule and transcript for credit. The student will have to complete withdrawal paperwork for the college and the institution will apply an appropriate grade to the student’s college transcript.
notes: program. Eligibility requirements for VT DE: Be enrolled as a junior or senior at CMHS; Be a resident of the State of Vermont; Not have taken more than 2 DE courses (available beginning the summer after the 10th grade year through the 12th grade year of high school); Earn a minimum score of 40 (math), 80 (reading) and 80 (writing) on the Accuplacer Assessment. Certain previous DE or RS courses or the CCV course: Intro to College and Careers may waive this requirement; Students must apply for a free payment voucher.

course_name: Early College at Your High School (EC)
description: The majority of DE opportunities are offered through White Mountain Community College’s (WMCC) Early College at Your High School (EC) program (formerly known as Running Start) through the Community College System of NH (CCSNH). Students receive high school credit for these courses offered at CMHS; however, students must request an official college transcript from the issuing institution to show the college credit. The courses are taught by high school teachers who meet the hiring qualifications for CCSNH faculty, and the course work and materials meet the college level content standards. These classes are weighted as Level 4: Dual Enrollment and are designated on transcripts with “RS”. Students enrolled in an Early College in Your High School course MUST engage in the college’s curriculum; however, the student may elect NOT to earn the college credits. The registration fee for each Early College at Your High School course is $150 and is paid for by the Canaan School District. A student who fails an Early College at Your High School course or withdraws from it after the add/drop deadline will have to reimburse the school district the $150 course fee. At the beginning of the semester, a representative from White Mountains Community College meets with all students scheduled for Early College at Your High School courses and explains the advantages of taking Early College/RS, the registration process, costs, etc.

description: The Fast Forward program allows Vermont residing students in CTE programs to get credit for college courses taken at regional CTE centers. Fast Forward is for Vermont students who have not yet graduated from high school and who are enrolled in a partner career technical education center program. The courses are taught at the regional CTE, and classes are scheduled during the regular school day. Each student is given two courses. Fast Forward helps students get high school and college credits (from either VTC or CCV), earn their degree faster, and start their career sooner. Students must request a voucher in the same way as Dual Enrollment.

description: Some colleges and universities in Vermont have developed an early admission program that allows high school seniors to take a full year of college-level classes while earning their high school diploma. The ECP simultaneously serves as a student's senior year of high school and a full year of college credit. Students enrolled in ECP are not eligible for Valedictorian or Salutatorian status. Students may take a year-long course of study in any discipline. The following have been approved to offer an ECP for the upcoming year: Castleton State University, Community College of Vermont, Goddard College, Johnson State College, Lyndon State College, Norwich University and Vermont Technical College (Vermont Academy of Science and Technology (VAST). description: The Virtual Learning Academy Charter School is New Hampshire’s first statewide, online school that is available, free of charge, to all middle and high school students who live in New Hampshire. The Academy also serves out-of-state students on a tuition basis. The Academy has been approved as a public charter school by the New Hampshire Board of Education and is also a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization. An independent Board of Trustees governs the school. CMHS’ students who are residents of NH can enroll in a VLACS course at any time during their academic career. Grades earned in VLACS courses are calculated into a student’s GPA based on the level of difficulty indicated by VLACS. Students can elect to take AP courses from VLACS and these would be Honors. description: Work-based learning experiences are an opportunity for students to apply academic, technical and employability skills in a work setting. These opportunities particularly help students make the connection between academic principles and real-world applications. For many, understanding “Why do I need to know this?” provides motivation for more learning. WBL experiences are available to all students as a way to explore academic and career areas of interests. While WBL experiences are intended to coincide with a CTE program (at which time the grade would be weighted as Honors), they can also be set up in areas of interest outside of a CTE program (at which time the grade would be weighted as Standard). Depending on what tasks and learning objectives are a part of the WBL, students can be paid or not paid for their WBL program. Students and their families will be responsible for transportation to the WBL. Students who are interested in WBL should notify the School Guidance Counselor of his/her intentions when registering for courses in the semester prior to when the internship is to begin. They may work together to identify and secure a WBL site. Prior to beginning the WBL experience, an agreement between the school, the WBL site, the student and parents will be completed and a supervisor at the WBL site identified. WBL will be closely monitored by the School Guidance Counselor. Grades for WBL will be based on weekly activity logs, twice a semester site supervisor evaluations and an online course through VtVLC “Workplace and Internship Readiness”.
notes: program. Grades for WBL are weighted Honors when coinciding with a CTE program, Standard otherwise (per catalog text).

description: CMHS students have the opportunity to participate in online courses through Virtual High School (VHS) or Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative (VtVLC). Students can take these online courses for the purposes of enrichment, not to fulfill requirements, unless extenuating circumstances exist. They are assigned to a supervised location and work independently. Courses must be pre-approved by the School Guidance Counselor, who also monitors the course. These courses are typically worth ½ credit. The add/drop period for these courses is the same as a regular course. Freshmen are discouraged from taking online courses due to the need of working independently; however, this will be determined on an individual basis. Also, if a student fails one online class, it is highly likely the student will not be able to take any additional online classes. VHS’ course offerings can be viewed at: https://vm3.vhslearning.org/catalog and VtVLC’s course offerings are located at: https://vtvlc.maestrosis.com/RS_FEViewCourses.aspx.

course_name: Northeast Kingdom Learning Services (NEKLS) & the High School Completion Program (HSCP)
description: HSCP allows our students to carve out their own path to high school graduation by working collaboratively with CMHS and NEKLS, Inc. to create a plan that meets Vermont state graduation requirements as well as individual student goals. Starting with the student’s CMHS’ transcript as a baseline, students can integrate courses, learning competencies, projects, employment, college courses, etc. to ultimately earn their CMHS diploma. To be in the program, students must be at least 16-years-old, pass HSCP testing standards, still be connected academically in some way to CMHS, and be recommended by the school. If a student or the family is interested in HSCP as a means to earn the diploma, a meeting should be scheduled with the School Guidance Counselor to complete a referral form. This form is reviewed and approved by a team which can include the Superintendent, Principal, School Guidance Counselor, Director of Student Services and Learning Plan Manager. Because of the individual nature of these learning plans, it is possible for students to meet their graduation requirements earlier than other seniors in June. If this happens, students are still required to continue any courses at CMHS they are enrolled in. During the time they have been in HSCP, students will work with the School Guidance Counselor to explore and secure a Work-based Learning experience.
notes: program

The in-vehicle driving is graded as Pass/Fail and is done during the student's free blocks during regular school hours. Students are required to have at least one free block in order to register for the course. Each student must demonstrate and meet the objectives of each driving lesson in order to pass. Students are expected to have a classroom average of 80%, attend 30 hours of classroom instruction, and meet the above in-vehicle driving requirements in order to be eligible to receive the Vermont Department of Motor Vehicles course completion card, or commonly referred to as the "Yellow Card.” Students are placed in Driver’s Ed by birthday with the oldest students having priority. Students must have their permit on their first day of class to be eligible for the course. Students are recommended to have a free block outside of the class itself in order to have adequate time to complete the driving portion of the course. All in-vehicle driving must be completed by the end of the course.

Tenth Grade Humanities is an interdisciplinary team-taught course where, upon successful completion, students earn full-year credit in both social studies and English. The history curriculum traces American experiences from European colonialism (1760s) all the up to the end of World War I (1918). The English curriculum functions as a thematic complement to the historical content through various works, including stories, novels, poems, songs, and articles. Sophomores will explore various humanities themes and topics including, Revolution, Civic Responsibility, Antebellum America, post-Civil War America, and American Expansion. In addition, tenth-graders will practice and develop a range of skills. These include developing claims, selecting and vetting evidence, extending analysis, engaging with text – as well as critical thinking and communicating through various modes of expression such as discussing, writing, presenting, and creating media. Teachers strive to meet students where they are in their lives and skill sets and to challenge them to be better critical thinkers, writers, communicators, and engaged citizens in a democratic society.
fulfills_text: Grade 10 Humanities - American Studies (required course); 2.0 credits (1.0 English, 1.0 Social Studies)

Seniors who have taken Writing Comp during their junior year will benefit from taking CCV English Composition, but a student who has already taken a college-level writing course should not take this course. description: Social Communication is a Unified class and is designed to provide all students with the tools to consider, discuss, and put into practice the fundamentals of one-to-one, small group, and one-to-many communication. In order to better understand communication both as a concept and as something we experience in our everyday lives, we will examine why we communicate (theory) and how we communicate depending on audience and purpose (skills). This course is intentionally designed to bring together students with and without disabilities.

In this elective English course, students will study past and present voices that define American literature and are relevant to life in 21st Century America. Our journey will begin in the mid 19th Century learning about the philosophy of Transcendentalism and its central tenets of self-reliance, non-conformity, free-thought, and the significance of the individual’s relationship with Nature. Moving forward in time in American history, students may explore the literary movements of Naturalism, Realism, and Modernism. Central themes include power, wealth, class, gender, race, and the American dream. Students will examine short fiction, non-fiction, poetry, novels, music, film, and art. Skills and assessments include close-reading, critical thinking, discussion, and analytical and creative writing.

Gothic Sci-Fi is a unique course that allows us to explore the wild and weird edges of the human mind in a relevant and current way. Specifically, we will embark on a quest to understand how Fear is both a function of biology and also of culture: If Fear is a biological and emotional reaction to the possibility of harm, then why do we love scary movies or horror video games and stories? How have different social taboos and fears around race and gender identity influenced the stories we tell, and what new trends in storytelling are emerging to challenge the colonialist themes in Western Science Fiction? There is a lot to be learned about separate types of fear, the long and short-term physiological impacts of fear, and how throughout history humans have processed those fears through the "Speculative Fiction" genre, which includes Afrofuturism, Science Fiction, Indigenous Futurism, Alternative History, Gothic, Horror, and Dystopian stories.

This course is for students who love to read, discuss, and write about great works of literature. AP teachers design thematic units that combine poetry, drama, short fiction, and novels. Students considering AP English must be capable of college-level work and should be prepared for a rigorous study of challenging, complex literature, an intense workload, and a rapid pace. Teachers emphasize critical thinking and analytical skills across reading, writing, and discussion assignments. All students must complete a series of summer assignments (including reading, annotating, and writing). Students may – but are not required to – take the AP English exam. Students may also be eligible for 3 college credits from St. Michael’s College through CVU’s dual enrollment program.
prerequisites: Summer reading and writing assignments. Students interested in taking the course during junior year are encouraged to discuss this option with their school counselor and 10th-grade English teacher.

description: This course is designed for students who want to learn more about the art of telling stories. Through literature and film, students explore the techniques and tools that express stories, analyzing the details of narrative and film –shot composition, lighting, and symbolism– providing students the opportunity to write, script, storyboard and film original stories.

Students write numerous fiction, creative nonfiction, and poetry pieces. Students read a variety of materials ranging from peer writing to published works. The class functions with the expectation that students participate in workshops, discussions, critiques, and public readings. Students hone their editing and revision skills.

description: In Global Literature, students examine how authors around the world and in various historical periods have grappled with the idea of what it means to be human. This course focuses on concepts of culture and identity and challenges students to think about their place in the international community. Students will be required to read a large number of texts, including novels, short stories, poetry, and biographies. Consistent participation in full-class discussions will be expected.

This course is a journey through the classic and contemporary literature of heroes and monsters. We explore how stories have captured the clash between good and evil and how that art has shaped the world we see around us. Through the study of specific literary techniques, themes, and conventions, close-reading, and various analytical, personal, and creative writing assignments, students will gain an appreciation for the function that stories of heroes and monsters serve society, and how these tales reflect what it means to be a human. Assessments will cover reading, writing, and speaking skills.

This elective English course allows students to experience diverse texts written by women across history and cultures. Readings will explore how gender, race, culture, beauty standards, and familial expectations shape identity. In addition, students will learn how women writers have responded to power dynamics and oppression throughout different time periods and waves of feminism. Students will examine short fiction, non-fiction, myths, poetry, novels, art, and film. Skills and assessments include close-reading, critical thinking, discussion, and analytical and creative writing.

This course will explore social justice through a literary and environmental lens. You'll investigate how social values shape our relationship with land and resources and how writers have explored these issues in various ways, from poetry to fiction to journalism. It's a chance to slow down and explore your relationships to the natural world, to your community, to yourselves, and to the issues that arise from your interactions with all of those as we focus on the important issues of climate change, environmental racism, and the role of activism in creating positive momentum. You'll examine local, American, and global perspectives on what it means to be human in a changing landscape and read fundamental literature about place, justice, and environmental advocacy. We'll engage in discussion, reading, and writing, and our classes will meet outside as much as possible.

Students read, research, analyze, and discuss utopian and dystopian elements of society through the study of complex literature. The class demands from students that they be careful and thoughtful readers, that they enjoy sharing and researching ideas, and that they can self-organize and self-manage their responsibilities.
