description: Windows and Mirrors, your 9th grade English class, begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate ourselves and others through a range of literature. We will learn how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, we will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, and use evidence, reasoning, and elaboration to support our thinking.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (9th grade English)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: In Sports and Adventure Literature, students will learn about themes that transcend specific texts, develop analytical and descriptive writing skills, understand the formal techniques and structure of sports and adventure texts and work individually and collaboratively to explore themes and techniques used by writers. Roughly one quarter will be dedicated to sports literature and the second quarter will focus on adventure literature.
prerequisites: None
notes: Listed as an elective for grades 9-12 in the English department chart (semester).

description: Intergenerational Book Club is a project-based class partnering Harwood students with seniors in the community to choose, read, and discuss books. The course is designed to build bridges across time and space, connecting young and more experienced community members around the acts of reading, talking, and writing about books. Students should expect to play an active role in their learning by designing, planning, and facilitating community bookgroup meetings. We will balance class time between working with books, corresponding with community partners, planning upcoming events, and reflecting on how we are meeting our goals.
prerequisites: None

description: What does it mean to be American? What are the values that we share versus the enduring tensions in our society? In this discussion-based course, students will study American fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and plays to better understand our nation and its heritage. We will examine the historical context of each piece that we read, and will often consider how the ideas of the authors speak to or contrast with current events.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (10th grade English)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: The primary goal of this semester-long English course is to become leaders in the design and practice of Harkness pedagogy and bring student-driven inquiry to the greater Harwood community. Just as important are the life skills you take away from this class, including honing your critical thinking (in reading, writing and reflection), public speaking, and ability to work as a team to innovate and problem solve.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English
notes: Department chart lists it as an elective for grades 10, 11 and 12 (semester only); course entry states Grade: 10, 11.

description: Why does news matter? In this course we explore its importance to democracy, its relationship to the First Amendment, and media ethics. This is a hands-on course; we will read and evaluate news in many forms, but we will also put out our own products in digital editions of “Common Ground,” photo essays, and podcasting. These pieces will reflect the interests of you, your classmates, and our greater Harwood community. The philosophy for our journalistic efforts can be summed up in one simple phrase: for students, by students, about things that students care about.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English

description: This year-long course is designed to build your creative writing and reading skills with a focus on creative nonfiction, short-fiction, and poetry. You will be asked to read, discuss, and analyze exemplary works of literature as well as create and respond to your own and your classmates’ work. In this class, you will explore a variety of ways to create meaningful pieces of writing. You will also have the opportunity to extend your audience beyond the classroom.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English OR a recommendation from a 9th grade English teacher
notes: Department chart: requires teacher recommendation (10th grade).

description: In this hands-on class, students will be actively learning how to write for business. They will analyze and write about business transactions as well as reading literature about famous businessmen and women and historical booms and collapses. We will look at socially responsible companies such as Ben & Jerry's and Darn Tough Socks Vermont and analyze their advertising and marketing communication through media literacy messaging.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English or a recommendation from 9th grade English teachers (10th graders)

description: This semester-long course examines master storytellers of mystery fiction and the art and craft of writing mystery fiction in its many forms, including detective stories, thrillers, and suspense. The goal is to understand and model the concepts of adventure, keeping secrets, and high octane suspense. Students can expect to read, discuss, and write mystery fiction in this course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: How can ancient stories inform our world today? What commonalities do we see among combatants and non-combatants in the stories told across eras? War Stories begins with the foundational Western war story, Homer’s Iliad, and then follows war storytelling to contemporary society. In this course, we uncover the tragedy and glory of the Greeks’ epic battle with Troy and its parallels to contemporary warfare. Our materials include Stanley Lombardo’s translation of Iliad paired with Gareth Hinds’ graphic adaptation of it; Lysistrata, by Aristophanes; All Quiet on the Western Front, by Erich Marie Remarque; The Things They Carried, by Tim O’Brien; City of Thieves, by David Benioff, along with multiple short stories, excerpts, poetry, and films. Students are expected to take ownership of their own learning, do the work, and drive our classroom discussions and discoveries. We will look at our texts through six themes: courage and cowardice; women’s roles in war; old men say, young men do; brotherhood and bonds; good leadership/bad leadership; and honor and dishonor. With every source we read, view, or discuss, we will return to these themes. As an elective course, there will be LESS homework than a core content course, but do expect to read outside of class time. Be mindful that the course will read about and discuss difficult and mature content that is often uncomfortable.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: Whose stories are worth telling? Which parts of our lives are important? In this Harkness-based course, we will read, discuss, and write about the work of women writers. We will explore a variety of poems, song lyrics, short fiction, essays, videos, and novels. Discover what women’s voices have to teach you, and develop your own voice as you consider their impact!
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: The AP English Language and Composition course aligns to an introductory college-level rhetoric and writing curriculum, which requires students to develop evidence-based analytic and argumentative essays. Students evaluate, synthesize and cite research to support their arguments. Throughout the course, students develop a personal style by making appropriate grammatical choices. Students also discover and analyze rhetorical elements in non-fiction texts from many disciplines including: speeches, biographies, contemporary non-fiction, business, sports, graphic images and historical periods. Students who take the AP English Language and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: This course is designed to replicate an introductory college-level literary analysis course. Its goal is to engage students in the close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature, thereby deepening their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide both meaning and pleasure. The class is inquiry based and encourages students to delve deeply into the material, take ownership of their learning and drive our classroom discussions.In this course, students can expect to read novels, plays, short stories, and poetry, and discuss those works through student driven inquiry such as Harkness. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. Students who take the AP English Literature and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: The Global Studies experience begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate our identities, our historical moment and how we got here, and how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, students will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, conduct research, and use evidence and reasoning to support their own thinking. The goal of this course is to help students build communication, research, and critical thinking skills while developing their own sense of what it means to be a Global Citizen.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (9th grade social studies)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: What does it mean to be a citizen in a republic? In Three Democracies, we learn about the rise and fall of democracy in ancient Athens and Rome, making connections to the United States and the challenges that we face. Students consider timeless and timely questions about justice, leadership, political division, empire, and more. Importance is placed on applying lessons from the past to the present. This course features a combination of reading, reflection, discussion, projects, and writing.
prerequisites: U.S. History or equivalent
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
notes: One of three 11th grade required options (Three Democracies, Creating Sustainable Communities, AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

description: U.S. History helps students learn about the past events, peoples and ideas that make up the United States of America, from the Native American civilizations to the founding documents drafted in Pennsylvania to the Civil and the World Wars, always taking into account the rich and vibrant tapestry of people whose roots and culture hail from all over the world and thus contribute to the unique American story. Students will learn to research and evaluate evidence, including primary sources; they will learn how to put information and ideas into context and how to compare sources and various accounts of the past. Students work alone and together as they deepen their ability to read closely and annotate texts, engage in civil discourse, write short texts and longer essays, and create and teach each other with multimedia presentations. Finally, students will not only learn about the past; they will reflect on the issues facing the country in the present, always inspired by the question: “How does learning about the past help us better understand the present and make more informed choices about the future?” The course makes extensive use of primary and secondary readings, textbooks, and videos. Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: CSC is designed to help students understand how the U.S. political system really works (political literacy), how the media influences the political system (media literacy), how to develop and communicate an educated opinion on important public policies (critical literacy, argumentative writing, and civil discourse), and how to use the tools they have available to them to make change in their local and/or state-wide communities (action civics). Students should expect to do the following in this course: ●​ Analyze, mark-up, and annotate a variety of written and recorded texts and media sources ●​ Thoughtfully consider multiple perspectives through civil discourse, active listening, note-taking, and deliberative dialogue ●​ Communicate an educated opinion on a variety of current events and political issues ●​ Develop a plan for taking action on an issue they care deeply about and/or addressing a need in the community through active citizenship or social entrepreneurship This course is unique to Harwood Union High School. It is designed to be deeply relevant and responsive to both current events and student interest. The goal of this course is to help students become the type of citizens who are able to create more resilient, more equitable, more joyful, more just, and more sustainable communities, now and in the future.
prerequisites: US History or Equivalent
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
notes: One of three 11th grade required options.

description: Who are you? Why is your behavior similar to or different from other humans? Psychology is a social science that seeks to answer questions about human behavior and this course explores the latest, peer-reviewed research in an attempt to shed light on the mysterious world inside your head. In particular, we will explore what science has discovered about learning, memory, emotions, creativity, sensory perception, and much more. In the end, you’ll understand how your brain really works—and how to get the most out of it. Class activities, readings, and assignments are designed so students can reflect upon personal experiences and how psychology applies to all aspects of human life. Harkness dialogue and presentations are common summative assessments in this course. Psychology is a vastly broad topic encompassing a wide range of areas of study. Behavior, learning and memory, childhood development, language, and internal mental processes are just a few examples. Students should leave this course with an understanding of the brain and its processes, human behavior, the scientific method and ethics of experimentation, and the history and differing perspectives within the study of psychology.
prerequisites: None

description: Students will explore how advertising shapes culture, identity, and values — and how it can also promote health, well-being, and the common good. Through student inquiry and hands-on projects, students will learn to research, design, and launch media campaigns that make a positive social impact. Students will begin the semester by exploring how marketing and advertising have evolved over time before moving on to issues in contemporary media and advertising. Students will then work with a community partner to develop a media and marketing campaign, including some students who will work to “market” Harwood Union High School. Note: the idea for this course, as well as the curriculum, was co-created in collaboration with a number of current Harwood students who will also be serving as teaching assistants next year.
prerequisites: None

description: History on Film is a course where students view and analyze feature films and movies, documentaries, and other audio and visual media, along with printed source material. The purpose is to gain historical knowledge, ask probing questions, and develop an informed opinion on topics that increase one’s understanding about past, present, and future issues and events. The primary forms of assessment are film analysis and class discussions to evaluate student learning and understanding. Students will need to be comfortable respectfully sharing ideas, supported by evidence, within a large group. Other types of assessment include detailed film notes, written reflections, and individual and group projects and presentations.
prerequisites: None

description: This course explores major events and contemporary issues in the news, while seeking to understand how they have developed from a historical perspective. Students analyze news accounts in various sources: mainstream and more independent media, social media and other venues. Context is always important so the historical roots of these problems will be examined and questioned. As historians and critical media consumers we will also consider: What is the role of media in a democratic society? What makes the “news” and how do reporters and editors interpret events? Can we believe what we read, see, hear and “click”? Students will help guide the directions we take and we’ll look at and critically consider all of it: the mainstream TV channels and “newspapers,” credible “alternative” media outlets, original documents, social media, radio and podcasts and even some of the less-than credible sources, to make sure we understand how peoples’ ideas and opinions are shaped. Class activities are discussion-based, and students will be able to demonstrate their learning through class dialogue, reaction papers, original projects, and digital presentations.
prerequisites: None

description: Economic decisions impact our everyday lives. Understanding economics means thinking about how limited resources require us to make choices and evaluate one option against another. In this course, you will come to recognize that there are examples of economics all around you. You will see how these economic choices, from larger groups such as state and federal governments, to individual consumers, impact us every day. This course will examine the basic concepts of economics, the pros and cons of capitalism, communism, and socialism, the federal and state budget-making process, our growing national deficit, income inequality, the role of the government during a recession, as well as economics-related current events stories.
prerequisites: None

description: Street Law explores the laws in our streets, cities, and states. This course provides a general overview of law and the role that it plays in our society. Areas of focus include constitutional law, criminal law, civil rights, contract law, civil law, and family law. Students are given practical information, helpful in our law-saturated society. The textbook and the U.S. Constitution provide the basic framework for our understanding of laws. Current events provide realistic examples of how the law applies to human actions. Discussions and note-taking are expected, and student presentations on law-related topics are required. Students will also be expected to participate in a series of mock trials.
prerequisites: None

description: AP U.S. Government and Politics provides students with the skills and knowledge to be active citizens in our American Republic, as well as to prepare them for success in taking the AP Gov Exam. Students can expect to discuss current events, analyze graphs, write argumentative essays, complete projects, read Supreme Court cases, participate in Harkness discussions, and take practice AP Gov tests. One major goal in AP Gov is for students to learn about how our government is designed to operate in theory and to develop a clearer understanding of how it operates in practice.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR you may submit a written appeal to the History Department to take the course; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework
fulfills_text: Counts as an 11th grade required option (AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

description: AP European History is a survey overview of the development of modern Europe. The time period covered by the course is 1450 - the present day. The following is taken from the College Board’s Course Description: AP European History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university European history course. In AP European History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in four historical periods from approximately 1450 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons; and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: interaction of Europe and the world; poverty and prosperity; objective knowledge and subjective visions; states and other institutions of power; individual and society; and national and European identity. Students who take AP European History are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability, and trigonometry. Learn to find heights of tall objects. Explore problems about data. Solve problems using constraints. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Methods for writing and graphing linear equations ●​ And more! The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.
prerequisites: None

description: This course is designed for students who want to double up on math courses to provide additional challenges or to provide more opportunity for electives later in their high school career. This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability and trigonometry. These strands are unified in themed units and students will develop math habits of mind through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Probability & expected value The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.
prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an Quarter 3 course score of 3.3 or above in 8th grade math; Must successfully complete a set of online prerequisite tasks and a formative assessment. This will be assigned digitally in March and due in early April.; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period; Teacher recommendation will be considered in this decision
notes: Must be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 (in person).

description: This course addresses intermediate math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions and geometry. Explore exponents with Alice in Wonderland. Blast off some quadratic equations with fireworks. Maximize your geometric potential with the corrals unit. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Three forms of linear functions ●​ Methods for solving systems of equations ●​ Exponential relationships, properties of exponents, and logarithms ●​ Creation and transformation of quadratic functions to solve problems ●​ Surface area, volume, and trigonometry, and other elements of Euclidean geometry The goal of this course is to give students an intermediate understanding of algebra and geometry.
prerequisites: Students must have a proficient course score in either Integrated Math 1 (or be concurrently enrolled in IM 1 online and meet the criteria for the online course)

description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. This course is designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an overall course score of 3.3 or above in Integrated Math 1; Must have a self direction of 3.3 or above; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period (and/or Harwood math teacher recommendation)
notes: Designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person.

description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
prerequisites: Students must have a Proficient course score in Integrated Math 2

description: Do you dream of being an independent, financially stable adult? This will be one of the most important courses you will ever take. This course introduces the fundamentals and skills of personal finance including budgeting, types of credit, managing credit, investments and savings. Use of the calculator and computer technology is emphasized. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Behavioral Finance ●​ Income & Taxes ●​ Banking: Checking & Savings ●​ Paying for College ●​ Types of Credit ●​ Managing Credit ●​ Investing ●​ Risk Management ●​ Budgeting The goal of this course is to introduce students to financial topics and to give students the skills to make thoughtful financial decisions now and in the future. Personal Finance for College Credit: For the 2026 fall semester, there will be the option to take this course for college credit. Students must meet all the class requirements as the student taking this course for Harwood credit plus the following: ●​ Use one of their dual enrollment vouchers ●​ Complete two independent learning units/projects on insurance and budgeting ●​ Answer additional questions on each of their three in-class summatives Students taking the class for college credit will be enrolled in the same PF classes as those taking it for Harwood credit. This is a great opportunity for students to use their dual enrollment vouchers for an in-person class without having to leave our campus!
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1 OR Integrated Math 1 Online
notes: For the 2026 fall semester there is an option to take this course for college credit using a dual enrollment voucher (details in description).

description: Why is math important to you? How will it apply to your areas of interest and your future? Come explore these ideas in a project-based learning environment where you choose the math application that directly impacts you and the things you care about. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Math topics that are relevant to their interests ●​ Techniques and processes to solve complex scenarios ●​ Connections between different mathematical disciplines The goal of this course is for students to apply mathematical logic, problem solving techniques, and a variety of math content to solve applied problems. Students will see the relevance of math in their own lives!
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1
notes: Duration: Semester 1 Only

description: This course is designed for students who plan to take Calculus at Harwood the following year. This course is a continuation of algebra and geometry topics required for the study of Calculus. Particular emphasis is given to topics that are fundamental to a first course in calculus including trigonometry, logarithms, function notation and transformation, and graphing calculator techniques. This class is a condensed and fast paced version of precalculus. Students can expect to: ●​ Increase fluency in interpreting math representations including tables, graphs, equations, situations ●​ Increase fluency in algebraic manipulation of equations ●​ Learn about applications and properties of Logarithms, Inverse functions, Rational Functions and Trigonometric Functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for Calculus or AP Calculus. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Students are currently enrolled in Integrated Math 3 and are maintaining a proficient score OR have completed Integrated Math 3 with a proficient course score
notes: Duration: Semester 2 only

description: This course is designed for students who have completed three experiences of Integrated Mathematics and are seriously interested in further exploration of mathematics. Throughout this course, students will continue to engage in mathematical habits of mind while gaining a deeper understanding of function behavior, algebraic modeling and manipulation. This course can serve as a prerequisite class for Calculus (either at Harwood or at college) or as an advanced math elective. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Transformations and manipulations of functions as related to the four mathematical representations of functions (graphical, tabular, algebraic, verbal) ●​ In depth analysis of the following types of functions: Trigonometric functions, Polynomials, Rational functions, Exponential functions, Logarithmic functions, and Inverse functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for further studies of mathematics, such as Calculus, as well as other college level maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3

description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Generally, concepts are presented informally and intuitively as well as proven more formally. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral and Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I and Part II) The goal of this course is to prepare students for college level math classes. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus

description: Do you want to be able to watch the news or read an article and understand what’s really going on? This course will teach you to develop critical thinking and analytic skills in order to act as an informed consumer. This course will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics may include: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses The goal of this course is to introduce students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2

description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Calculus course to prepare students to take the Calculus AB Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Calculus are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral & Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I & II) ●​ Preparation for the AP Calculus Examination The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Calculus exam and other college maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND either Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework; If students are not proficient in AP Calculus by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Calculus.

description: The AP course in statistics will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Statistics course to prepare students to take the Statistics Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Statistics are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses ●​ Using inferences to determine when variables are related The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Statistics exam and provide a general understanding of statistical analysis. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2.; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework.; If students are not proficient in AP Statistics by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Statistics.

description: This performance-based class will study a variety of genres of music and participate in various concerts throughout the year. Together we will learn the fundamentals of music literacy, meaningful & expressive singing, and composition! All grades and experience levels are welcome. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for local, state, and regional music festivals, as well as an after-school honors choir.
prerequisites: None
notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

description: This course offers music students a large ensemble experience to build instrumental technique through the study and performance of varied musical styles including but not limited to contemporary concert band, 20th century rock, jazz, soul, funk, latin, experimental and film music. Performance skills, techniques, theory and varied music literature are explored. Students can expect to play concerts throughout the year and should have at least two years of reading music to enroll in this class. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for local, state, and regional music festivals. There is NO prerequisite for this course.
notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

description: This course is designed to create opportunities for students to engage in contemporary music performance both as a musician and/or crew member. The band regularly plays for school assemblies, community events, and various gigs in Vermont. Performing in the Assembly Band (guitar, bass, drums, keyboard, vocals, wind instrument) by teacher recommendation.
prerequisites: Auditions in the Spring
notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

description: In this year-long course, the primary charge is for students to build and operate a near-professional media production company that puts on a short production (assembly) every few weeks for the school community. Student tasks and responsibilities will vary depending on their particular job in the company. The jobs can be organized into the following categories: Pre-Production Staff and outreach: Script writer, social media manager, promotion, spirit committee, outreach Production Crew: Stage manager, stage crew, light design/operation, sound engineer, show hosts Film Crew: Camera operators, post-production editors
prerequisites: Interviews in the Spring
notes: Duration: Year-Long ELO Series

description: This course is designed for students who want to learn how to form their own band and develop a set of music. This is a great stepping stone for students who may ultimately perform in the assembly band. The course is open to vocalists and beginning to intermediate guitar, bass, keys and drum students. At the start of the semester, our focus will be on building technique through the learning of simple classic and modern rock songs. As we progress through the semester, we will explore original songwriting and how to craft our own arrangements of cover songs. The semester will culminate with a recording session and/or a live performance. Although welcome, no prior musical experience is required.
prerequisites: None
notes: Duration: Semester-Long ELO Series

description: This series approaches music theory through the lens of writing music. Intended for all students who are motivated to study music and interested in music, language, composition, technology, history, and performing.
notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

description: This series is designed for students interested in singing and performing contemporary vocal styles like pop, R&B, jazz, musical theater, rock, etc. All experience levels are welcome. Students will develop vocal technique through one-on-one and group instruction. Students will have opportunities to perform for each other as well as in the community.
notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

description: This series is for students interested in learning production techniques in electronic music. We will use a variety of music hardware and software to learn the art of DJing, and production, remixing, mashups, live looping, EDM, original composition, video game scoring. The experience will include a live performance/ presentation in the style of a DJ set and/or screening of their work. Although welcome, no prior musical experience is required, just an interest in producing, creativity and sharing new work.
notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

description: This laboratory science course will engage students in learning about the formation of the universe and the earth. Students will start by learning about the universe including the atoms that make it up, the Big Bang theory, as well as stellar evolution and nuclear fusion. Students will then learn about the history of the earth starting with how the solar system was made, to how it is constantly changing, and how we are able to know the ages of things on earth. Lastly, students will learn about the history of life on earth and scientific innovations that have shaped our lives so far. The goal of this course is to provide students with a foundation of science skills and science knowledge by covering Next Generation Science Standards in earth science, life science, and physical sciences.
prerequisites: None
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: This laboratory science course will engage students in learning about the different systems that play a part in our dynamic biosphere and atmosphere. We will focus on building our repertoire of science skills, including engineering design, reading informational texts, and designing experiments. Students will learn about energy, chemical reactions, cycles of matter, the oceans, the atmosphere, global climate change, and genetics. The goal of this course is to provide students with a foundation of science skills and science knowledge by covering Next Generation Science Standards in earth science, life science, and physical science.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: Come learn about how scientific knowledge and scientific experiments play a role in our legal system. We will design and conduct experiments relating to different types of evidence and also learn about how those types of evidence can be used to help solve crimes. This course will also look into the limitations of using forensic science and how it has led to wrongful convictions. *This elective class runs every other year
prerequisites: None

description: Have you ever wondered why you do the things you do? What drives your emotions and behavior? In Science of the Mind students will study the adolescent brain and how it influences adolescents' interactions with the world. Students will have the opportunity to learn about the biological structure, function, and development of the adolescent brain. Throughout this learning, students will build connections between the biological and social influences that lead to their everyday social, emotional, biological experiences and well being. *This elective class runs every other year
prerequisites: None

description: Come learn about how living things work! Investigate the inner workings of cells that make up all living things. Zoom in on DNA, the molecule of inheritance, to discover its role in determining our genetic traits. Then look at the world's ecosystems to see how these cellular and molecular systems interact on a global scale. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Biology concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Biology.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Biology.

description: Ready for some reactions? Come learn about the matter that makes up our world and how it relates to various phenomena such as oil spills and the Flint water crisis. This science laboratory course engages students in learning about what our world is made up of on the atomic and molecular level and how those particles interact with each other and change through chemical reactions. We will also learn mathematical applications that allow us to calculate the quantities of atoms and molecules in various substances and solutions, and learn how to model and explain various conceptual ideas relating to atoms, molecules and chemical reactions. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Chemistry concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of chemistry.
prerequisites: Successful Completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of chemistry.

description: Welcome to Physics! This course is designed as an algebra-based, introductory physics course where students look into the fundamental patterns of motion and forces. Students will learn about how the universe is governed by simple laws, which can be discovered through experimentation and graphical analysis. We will begin with the basics of motion and Newton’s Laws, and dive into energy and momentum. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Physics concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Physics.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Physics.

description: Advanced Placement Biology is a college level Biology course. Students will learn how to apply biological knowledge, problem-solving skills, and scientific thinking that can be utilized to take the AP Biology test. During this course students will delve deeper into intricate biological details, move at an accelerated rate, while demonstrating independence and self-direction. Students who take the AP Biology course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Successful completion of or co-registration in Chemistry; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: How can we meet the needs of a growing population while sustaining natural resources? How can the global community collaborate to address environmental challenges? What does science tell us about our relationship with and dependence on the earth? In AP Environmental Science, you’ll cultivate your understanding of the interrelationships of the natural world through inquiry-based lab investigations and field work as you explore concepts like the four Big Ideas; energy transfer, interactions between earth systems, interactions between different species and the environment, and sustainability. Students who take the AP Environmental Science course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: Are you ready for an intellectually challenging and rigorous college level course? Students will be completing the equivalent curriculum to a general chemistry class at a college or university, therefore it is a very fast paced course. Strong math and reasoning skills are needed for success in this course. This course will also require a good work ethic with independent motivation for students to study and learn material outside of class. It is estimated that students will be expected to complete 1 hour of studying/work per night for this course. The course will run for two blocks, which will include laboratory time, lecture time, and group problem solving time. Students who take the AP Chemistry course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Completion of Integrated Math 2; Successful completion of OR Co-enrollment in Integrated Math 3; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework
notes: Duration: Year-long, double block

description: AP Physics 1 is an algebra based, college level Physics course. Students will cultivate their understanding of physics through inquiry based experimentation, in class Harkness discussions, textbook readings and online homework. The course covers topics of projectile motion, forces, energy, momentum, simple harmonic motion, and torque and rotation. Students who take the AP Physics course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 & 2; Successful completion of Integrated Math 2; Successful completion of or co-enrollment in Integrated Math 3; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: AP Computer Science Principles introduces students to the world of computer programming which has many applications in a variety of career fields. Working with your classmates to address real world problems, you will use your creativity to design and develop a computer program that collects and manages data using efficient algorithms. No previous coding experience is required. AP Computer Science Principles is equivalent to a first-semester college computing course. Students who take the AP Computer Science Principles course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: IM1

description: Principles of Engineering (POE) is a foundation course of Project Lead The Way (PLTW) engineering pathway for high schoolers. This course explores a variety of engineering concepts to help students determine a potential pathway in engineering following high school. Through problems that engage and challenge, students explore a broad range of engineering disciplines, including mechanisms, materials, structures, circuits, and programming. The course applies and concurrently develops secondary level knowledge and skills in mathematics, science, and technology culminating in a final robotics project.
prerequisites: IM1

description: Game Design is a project based course to explore the world of computer game development. The course begins with guided tutorials in a game engine. After acquiring the needed skills, students will build a unique game using the iterative design process. Throughout the course, we will explore the qualities of successful games along with the many facets of design and engineering used in video game development.
prerequisites: None

description: This course will serve as an introduction to computer programming with basic algorithms. Students will utilize the Python programming language to develop an understanding of concepts such as variables, functions, and control structures as they analyze, write, and test code. This class is for beginners; no programming experience is required.
prerequisites: None

description: Previously called Designing Sustainability, this course aims to help students develop an engineering mindset, which can be used to design and promote sustainable solutions to some of the world’s largest problems. Potential topics include water purification, energy and waste, growing food, and technology. Through the study of systems dynamics, change theory, and public policy, students will begin to better understand the complex interactions between our environment, economy, and society, and develop critical skill sets they can use to create a more just, joyful, and sustainable community. Completion of this course can count as a semester science experience.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Completion of this course can count as a semester science experience.

description: This is a foundational art course with a focus on two-dimensional visual art (drawing, painting, and printmaking). Students will experiment with different art concepts and techniques, as well as many different materials. Each project allows students to personalize their work while engaging in the structure of new techniques/concepts/materials. *This is a prerequisite class for Art 2, Art for Harwood, and Advanced Studio Art.
prerequisites: None

description: This studio-based course introduces students to a variety of professional quality, functional artwork through experiencing a variety of traditional and nontraditional materials and methods. Students are encouraged to develop their own personal creativity and craftsmanship with hands-on projects. Projects are created with a variety of materials like clay, leather, and paper. *This is a prerequisite class for Pottery 1, Jewelry, and Ceramics
prerequisites: None

description: This class is a comprehensive introduction to software-based graphic design using Adobe Creative Suite. Successful advertising and design are instrumental in today’s multimedia-based economy. Learn the tools that professionals use in their day-to-day lives. Students dive into the elements of design, color theory, layout, text-based design, and image manipulation. Throughout the course, students will complete a diverse range of projects from logo designs, posters & magazine covers, to original low-poly portraits. The goal of this course is to become proficient in the elements and principles of design and Adobe Photoshop. *This is a prerequisite class for Digital Photography 1
prerequisites: None

description: Art 2 builds upon knowledge learned in Art I with an emphasis placed on: technical aspects of art creation and expressing ideas through a variety of styles and methods. This course is for students who want an opportunity to extend their understanding and skill development in the two-dimensional and even three-dimensional areas. *This is a prerequisite class for Art for Harwood, and Advanced Studio Art.
prerequisites: Proficient in Art 1

description: This class is for students who want to advance their personal development in the Digital Arts. Students who have successfully taken Graphic Design and Photo I (with a proficient score) are invited to dive deeper into the Digital Art world through a project-based environment that will enable greater freedom to explore, create, and find their own artistic voice. Using an individualized approach, students will work on projects based around Rebranding, Photo Restoration, Photojournalism, Commercial Photography, Marketing, and typography and fully exploring the interaction of text and image. This is a challenging and exciting class, which requires creative brainstorming, conceptualizing, critical thinking, collaboration, and presentation. The goal of this course is to gain confidence in your digital art skills as you advance your techniques while working with industry-standard equipment and programs.
prerequisites: Proficient in Graphic Design and Digital Photography 1

description: This course is an in depth exploration into clay, using various handbuilding techniques- pinch, slab and coil. Time is devoted to terminology, techniques, tools, and surface treatments, such as glazes and underglazes. All students cooperate in clay recycling as well as loading and unloading the kiln. Students are encouraged to develop their creativity and incorporate their own vision into each of their projects.
prerequisites: Proficient in Intro to Crafts

description: Advanced Studio Art is a course for independent students who want to strengthen their skills and experience in art. This offering is for students who (but not limited to): students who want to focus on a specific idea and/or medium, and/or students who want to develop a portfolio of their artwork for applying to college. This is a personalized course, therefore, students will work with the teacher on developing projects, setting goals, documenting work, taking part in class critiques and setting up the art show.
prerequisites: Proficient in Art 1 and Art 2 OR Art 1 and permission from teacher

description: This course introduces students to various processes of jewelry making. Students will be exploring materials such as wire, glass, clay and metal to create their designs. Students will create earrings, pendants, bracelets and rings from a variety of techniques and materials. Historical and contemporary processes will be explored with an emphasis on design and craftsmanship.
prerequisites: Proficient in Intro to Crafts

description: Learn the basics of the potter’s wheel, such as centering, opening, pulling, shaping and trimming vessels such as bowls, mugs and covered jars. Students assist in loading and unloading the kiln and complete all of their projects with glaze. Learn through step by step instructions and demonstrations. Individual creativity and development are encouraged through the creation of functional and decorative projects. *This is a prerequisite class for Pottery 2
prerequisites: Proficient in Intro to Crafts

description: This is an intensive course for students who are serious about their continued growth and experiences on the potter’s wheel. This class is a continuation of Pottery I and reviews basic information about clay, wheel throwing, glazes and kiln technology and expands on these skills and techniques. This course will focus on the student’s aesthetic and technical development in the creation of larger and more complex wheel-thrown functional pieces.
prerequisites: Proficient in Pottery 1

description: This comprehensive introduction to the photographic medium includes both the building of technical skills, as well as finding one’s creative voice in visual art. Students will learn how to manually photograph with school provided DSLR cameras, discover the Elements & Principles of photography, learn how to edit with top of the line editing software and print their finished work. Class projects will exhibit the unique and relevant vision that every student has as observers of the human experience. Students are also continually introduced to past and present artists as they begin to develop their own personal style and vision as a photographer. The goal of this course is to become proficient in digital photography through the understanding of: manual camera settings and functions, the elements and principles of design and how they contribute to successful photographs, editing, printing and critiquing your own work. *This is a prerequisite class for Digital Photography 2 & Advanced Digital Art
prerequisites: Proficient Graphic Design

description: This continuation of Photography I enables students to further develop their personal vision in photography within a project-based learning environment. Having mastered the importance of the foundational processes in Photo I, this class enables students greater freedom to explore and create their own voice through advanced technical skills, collage, mixed media, and alternative processes. Students will also learn the critical skills needed to build a portfolio of multiple visual art pieces within personalized project design.
prerequisites: Proficient in Graphic Design & Digital Photography 1

description: This course is designed to provide students a basic introduction of skills and knowledge for the different ways one can be physically active for now and the future based on the classes that are offered here at Harwood: CardioWeight Training, Outdoor Adventure, Teaching Games for Understanding, Individual/Dual Activities, and Move & Groove. Students can expect to learn and experience the physical, social and emotional benefits of being physically active in different forms. Throughout the semester students will have the opportunity to learn, explore, and experience working individually, with partners, in small and large groups and how groups form and function based on the stages of group development. Using the activities implemented in class as evidence, students will report on the characteristics of each stage of group development (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing and Adjourning). The goal of this course is to ensure all students have a solid base towards their physical literacy journey (introduction of all PE classes) while also building up on their social emotional learning skills (Reviewing the 5 stages of Group Dynamics) to help influence one’s communication skills within a group to enhance their ability to be active outside of school and moving forward as adults. This is the prerequisite class for students to then choose which class(es) they want a deeper level of skills and knowledge towards.
prerequisites: This course is required in 9th grade before taking any other PE course.
fulfills_text: This course is required in 9th grade before taking any other PE course.
notes: Wellness chart lists it as "Foundations for Physical Education (PE)".

description: Students will participate in single, partner and team activities through a Teaching Games for Understanding approach. Skills and Strategies will be broken down based on the category that the activity falls under. Games/Activities may include: ●​ Target Games - Archery, Disc Golf, Ball Golf, Bocce, Cornhole, Ladder Ball, Kan-Jam, Bowling. ●​ Net/Wall Games - Volleyball, Badminton, Pickleball, Table Tennis, Spikeball, Nitroball, Eclipseball ●​ Invasion Games - Flag football, Basketball, Floor Hockey, Flag Rugby, Ultimate Frisbee, Capture the Flag ●​ Striking and Fielding Games - Kickball, Wiffleball, Baseball/Softball, Cricket Activities offered will depend on weather, class enrollment and availability of facilities. Students will develop independent learning skills as well as team skills while supporting each other towards being physically active. They will also gain an understanding of lifetime activities and the influence games have on physical, social, and emotional health.

description: Students will participate in single/partner/small group activities such as archery, badminton, tennis, pickleball, table tennis, volleyball, golf, circus skills, disc golf, bowling, orienteering, snowshoeing, and lawn games. description: In this course, students will be introduced to the major characters and stories of ancient Greek and Roman mythology. In doing so, students will explore such questions as: What is myth? Why do societies create myths? How does mythology shape thought and culture? Students will also analyze the legacy of classical myth in art, literature, film, and theater, from the plays of Shakespeare to the modern musical Hadestown. Throughout the course, building an argument, both in writing and in discussion, using literary and artistic evidence from our sources, will be emphasized.
prerequisites: None

description: In French 1, the emphasis is all about understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials .The main goal of this course is to learn the basics of the French language. Listening and speaking skills are a prime concern, thus the emphasis is on meaningful communication in everyday situations. Students practice grammar, vocabulary, and idioms orally and then have these skills reinforced in reading and writing. Students enjoy an introduction to the French-speaking world through slides, videos, storytelling, and discussion.
prerequisites: None

description: This is the second level of French offered at Harwood. The emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. It is a critical level, designed to increase the student’s fluency and confidence in the language through continued reading, vocabulary enrichment, listening, oral practice and cultural awareness. Students improve their speaking in French through role-playing everyday situations in both guided and open conversation as well as through direct dialogue. Both reading and listening comprehension are reinforced and expanded using different types of resources. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, songs, and cooking.
prerequisites: Completion of French 1 or department approval
notes: Chart: students who completed French 1 in 7th/8th grade begin with French 2 in 9th grade.

description: In French 3, the emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. At the same time, students are also encouraged to grapple more with language patterns and grammatical structures, and apply them to their speech and writing. This can be a pivotal year which can encourage students to continue pursuing language study thanks to the curiosity and confidence it can provide, while pushing the rigorous demands of this level of language.
prerequisites: Completion of French 2 or department approval

description: At the fourth level of French offered at Harwood, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in French at an intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open. Their listening competency is addressed using various recordings and videos. Students improve their reading in French using authentic short stories (written and/or visual). Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations and songs, and hopefully penpal communication and visit?!
prerequisites: Completion of French 3 or department approval

description: At the fifth level of French, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in French at an upper-intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open, as well as through student-led Harkness discussions. Expectations are that French will be spoken 90%+ of the time. Emphasis is placed on discovering and analyzing current events. Students improve their reading in French using authentic sources and materials. Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations, song and cooking. Students who take the AP French course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam. *In addition, seniors will be eligible for the Seal of Biliteracy. The Seal of Biliteracy is an award given by the Vermont Organization of Classics and Language Educators under the authorization of the Agency of Education in recognition of students who have studied and attained proficiency in two or more languages [including English] by high school graduation. The Seal of Biliteracy takes the form of a seal that appears on the transcript or diploma of the graduating senior and is a statement of accomplishment for future employers and for college admissions. More information will be provided by World Language teachers.
prerequisites: Completion of French 4 or department approval

description: This one-semester class provides a foundation for 9th graders to do self-exploration about who they are as individuals. Emphasis is placed on discovering their interests, skills, and strengths and connecting them to personal, educational, and professional goals and/or pathways. Students will learn how to communicate professionally by creating a résumé, participate in a mock interview, and write a professional thank you letter; research careers of interest and connect their personal interests to career fields; and begin to plan a roadmap through high school that allows them to pursue flexible pathways and classes that are connected to their interests.

description: Building off students’ previous experience in DSH middle school courses, this class will utilize food and “systems thinking” as a means to understanding the three primary aspects of sustainability: social equity, economic fairness, and environmental health. In this project-based course, students will spend much of the semester developing culinary and marketing skills through food production and distribution connected to Harwood’s “Harvest of the Month” programming and other school-wide events. Students will also participate in group activities and field trips that examine the impact of social and environmental systems on the individual, their immediate community, and the larger world. Finally, this course will utilize guest speakers to provide students with first-hand perspectives on potential career tracks related to the culinary, service, agricultural, health, and public policy industries.
prerequisites: None

description: Is there something you wish you could do, learn, experience, or make at school? In Idea Lab, students will be supported to design, experience, and make their own projects. This could look like designing and prototyping a product, learning a new skill or craft (or leveling up an existing one), taking a deep dive into researching a topic of interest, or pursuing a project related to a club or extracurricular activity. Students will explore interests, ask questions, research their topic, connect with community experts, manage time, document their progress, set goals, prioritize their work, and most importantly spend time developing their project artifact. Class takes place in the Exploratory Lab where students will have access to a variety of high and low tech tools and materials.This class will not only let you learn what you want, but will teach you the career and college ready skills you need to organize and manage long term projects.
prerequisites: None
notes: Duration: Semester, can be taken multiple times

description: Documenting the World, a course supporting the amazing travel opportunities offered at Harwood, will provide students with a project-based opportunity to deeply explore the immensely complex concept of CULTURE: How is it created? How do we consume it? How does it impact ourselves and the way we view the world? In this semester course open to ALL grade levels, students will first spend time digging into their own experiences to examine these broad questions through community interviews and the development of multimedia-based stories. As the class progresses, the focus shifts to the discipline of cultural anthropology and the skills of ethnographic inquiry; students will be introduced to the rich cultures of each destination visited by Harwood’s travel study program - Denmark, Columbia, Rwanda, and India. Ultimately, this course is designed to provide participants with a window into the world of others and reinforce the idea that culture is much more than a set of unique values and behaviors that divide us from one another. The more we explore diverse cultures, the more we realize just how similar our lived experiences are.
prerequisites: None

description: Career and Personal Planning (CPP) is designed to reinforce and refine the habits-of-being necessary for success in the world beyond high school. In CPP, students will be given space to explore potential ways to take that “next step” after graduation and set post-secondary goals that are personally significant to their educational and/or career aspirations. Because the class has been developed in conjunction with Community College of Vermont’s “Intro to College & Career” course, CPP students will also officially enroll at CCV, utilize the college’s digital learning platform, and earn a non-degree-bearing credit for successfully completing the course; however, it will NOT count towards a student’s 2 dual-enrollment opportunities. description: Interested in working with your classmates as entrepreneurs to run a business? Through hands-on activities, student-led business opportunities and a culminating pitch project, students will gain real-world experience turning ideas into viable business ventures that turn a profit. In Adventure in Business you will: ●​ Use creative and critical thinking skills to imagine a product or service that meets a community need. ●​ Develop a business plan using collective skills and available resources. ●​ Participate in management positions of interest such as marketing, product development, sales, advertising or communications. ●​ Launch, operate and evaluate the success of your student run business and/or personal business plan. ●​ Collaborate with small business owners, entrepreneurial experts and the Vermont Small Business Development Center. ●​ Practice presentation skills culminating in a formal business plan pitch. ●​ Explore future career interests and opportunities in entrepreneurship and small business.

description: The Harwood Community Learning Center is a personalized, community-based program open to all juniors and seniors at Harwood. Students enrolled in this daily, double-block experience receive English, history, science, math and elective (career exploration) credits. HCLC attempts to approach education holistically. Classes balance experiential and traditional learning models while also providing both individualized and group-oriented academic instruction. The program is built around long-term, interest-based projects. As students move through the interdisciplinary project structure, they conduct research, access community experts, and gather resources best suited to the development of a final product that showcases new learning in an authentic way. At its core, HCLC provides students with the following: 1.​ A small, tight-knit learning community where students are approached as individuals 2.​ A flexible educational environment that incorporates student interest into core academics and provides ample one-on-one support 3.​ A focus on future planning to help students get organized for their life after high school

description: Wayfinding is a course designed to assist students in exploring options for life after high school. Whether you’re thinking about joining the workforce, are college bound, taking a gap year, traveling abroad, or you’re not at all sure of your direction, this course will open up possibilities and help to guide you towards your path. Students will engage in multiple activities such as interest inventories, personality tests, a reality game, a values auction, and a values assessment in order to help align them with possible career paths. There are multiple opportunities to hone verbal communication skills, such as through informational interviews and presentations. Students will read Tuesdays with Morrie and The Last Lecture.

Reading and Writing to Challenge the Status Quo: This class will center around themes of censorship and intellectual freedom as students read and analyze literature of a variety of genres, including contemporary novels, historical fiction, science fiction,fantasy and literature with futuristic views of the world. We will examine how literature often critiques the society we live in, and gives much food for thought on why we do the things we do, and maybe why we should change those things. We will study the author's craft, design and structure, and analyze the text to better understand how master authors write to communicate messages.Students will have opportunities to create their own reading lists and personalize their learning around social issues and actions of importance to them.

This course will be a broad survey of philosophical topics, such as logical reasoning & argumentation, truth & knowledge, and ethics. The course will involve a great deal of discussion, debate, and persuasive writing.

Dare To Be Me is for students who like to be active, get outside, breathe fresh air, and engage their hearts, senses, bodies, and minds. As its title suggests, the focus of the course is on being rather than doing. By blending time in Nature with physical exercise, mindfulness, quiet introspection, meaningful, in-depth conversations and creative journaling, DTBM students learn to understand themselves better and develop the courage to lean into who they want to become. They will grow their ability to be present, curious, grateful, empathetic, adaptable and resilient even in times of adversity while identifying their passions, advancing their emotional literacy, and beginning to articulate and embody their values and purpose. The class prioritizes holistic wellbeing and self-discovery and is built on the philosophy that students who are self-aware, grounded, and balanced can access any kind of learning at a much deeper level. It is therefore a perfect complement to any other class while teaching essential life and transferable skills.
